title: When AUC Meets Generative Reconstruction: A Unified Principle for Balanced Visual Representation Learning

AI.tldr: This paper reformulates generative reconstruction as a discriminative ranking problem within the generative output manifold, proposing AUCGR and pAUCGR to balance discriminative and fine-grained perceptual visual representation learning.
AI.motivation: MLLMs require visual encoders with both fine-grained perceptual features and semantically disentangled discriminative representations, yet contrastive learning suppresses intra-class variability while generative reconstruction lacks comparative supervision, and naively combining their losses causes gradient interference.
AI.method: The authors propose AUC Generative Reconstruction (AUCGR), which optimizes the area under the ROC curve by ranking matched reconstruction outputs above mismatched ones, and Partial AUC Generative Reconstruction (pAUCGR), which focuses mismatched comparisons on reliable feature subspaces in a plug-and-play manner without architectural changes.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis connects the objectives to AUC/pAUC optimization with generalization guarantees, and experiments across diverse CLIP architectures, over 30 visual benchmarks, generative backbones, and MLLMs show consistent gains in both discriminative accuracy and fine-grained perceptual representation.
AI.conclusion: Reformulating generative reconstruction as discriminative ranking resolves loss competition between contrastive and generative objectives, setting a new benchmark for balanced visual representation learning.

title: ZIP: Scalable Crowd Counting via Zero-Inflated Poisson Modeling

AI.tldr: This paper proposes ZIP, a scalable crowd counting framework that models blockwise counts using a Zero-Inflated Poisson likelihood, consistently outperforming state-of-the-art methods across model scales on standard benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing crowd counting methods regress blockwise density maps with Mean Squared Error (MSE) losses, which dilute supervision signals due to extreme spatial sparsity (over 95% of 8x8 blocks are empty) and rely on a Gaussian error model ill-suited for discrete, non-negative count data.
AI.method: ZIP models blockwise counts with a Zero-Inflated Poisson likelihood, where a zero-inflation term learns the probability of a structurally empty block and a Poisson component models expected counts when people are present.
AI.result: Generalization analysis shows a tighter risk bound for ZIP than MSE-based losses and DMCount at moderately large training resolutions; across backbones spanning over 100x in parameters/compute, ZIP surpasses state-of-the-art methods on ShanghaiTech A & B, UCF-QNRF, and NWPU-Crowd.
AI.conclusion: Modeling crowd counts with a Zero-Inflated Poisson likelihood provides a theoretically grounded and scalable alternative to MSE regression for crowd counting.

title: Inversion-Free Style Transfer with Dual Rectified Flows

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an inversion-free style transfer framework using dual rectified flows that fuses content and style trajectories in a single forward pass.
AI.motivation: Mainstream training-free diffusion-based style transfer methods rely on computationally expensive inversion processes that reduce efficiency and introduce visual distortions when inversion is inaccurate.
AI.method: The framework predicts content and style trajectories in parallel using dual rectified flows, fuses them via dynamic midpoint interpolation that adapts to the evolving stylized image, and applies attention injection to guide style integration.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show that the method generalizes across diverse styles and content images while improving visual fidelity, content preservation, and computational efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Dual rectified flows with dynamic midpoint interpolation and attention injection enable effective and efficient inversion-free style transfer.

title: Gaussian Light Field Splatting: A Physical Prior-Driven Vision Transformer for Low-Light Image Enhancement

AI.tldr: This paper proposes GLFS, a Vision Transformer for low-light image enhancement that embeds continuous 2D Gaussian Splatting light-field priors into self-attention to guide spatial gain estimation.
AI.motivation: Existing low-light image enhancement methods suffer from local exposure imbalance and color distortion under non-uniform illumination, while mainstream Vision Transformers lack explicit physics-based priors for illumination degradation.
AI.method: GLFS represents scene illumination as a superposition of anisotropic Gaussian basis functions from 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS), injects this physical bias into self-attention to infer a spatial gain field, and trains with a color vector angular loss and a luminance edge loss.
AI.result: Extensive ablation studies and quantitative evaluations show that GLFS achieves competitive overall performance in illumination correction, structure preservation, and perceptual quality.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating continuous Gaussian light field priors into Vision Transformer self-attention is an effective physical prior for low-light image enhancement.

title: On the Existential Theory of the Reals Enriched with Integer Powers of a Computable Number

AI.tldr: This paper establishes decidability and complexity bounds for the existential theory of the reals enriched with integer powers of a computable real number when its algebraicity or transcendence is known.
AI.motivation: Deciding satisfiability in the existential theory of the reals with integer powers of a computable real number r > 0 is undecidable if only a Turing machine computing r is given.
AI.method: The authors design decision algorithms for cases where r is known to be transcendental or algebraic (a root of an integer polynomial) and analyze complexity using a polynomial root barrier property.
AI.result: Under a polynomial root barrier, satisfiability is in NEXPTIME for natural numbers, EXPSPACE for algebraic numbers, and 3EXP for a family of transcendental numbers including pi and Euler's e; as a by-product, the entropic risk threshold problem for stochastic games with base e and algebraic aversion factor is shown to be in EXP without assuming Schanuel's conjecture.
AI.conclusion: Knowing the algebraicity of r circumvents undecidability in this theory and yields unconditional complexity bounds for related stochastic game problems.

title: Epidemic control under incomplete observations through mechanistic state reconstruction and multi-agent learning

AI.tldr: This paper presents a three-stage computational epidemiology framework combining observation modeling, mechanistic state reconstruction (ODE-DynNet), and multi-agent reinforcement learning for epidemic control under incomplete surveillance.
AI.motivation: Epidemic-control policies trained on raw reported infection counts suffer from suboptimal testing and isolation decisions because reporting is distorted by varying testing capacity, delays, reporting behavior, and asymptomatic infections.
AI.method: The authors extend a metapopulation SEIQR model to represent different observability regimes, propose ODE-DynNet (combining mobility-coupled epidemic dynamics with graph-temporal learning) to reconstruct hidden infection states, and optimize testing and isolation via multi-agent reinforcement learning with a flow-based responsibility-aware reward.
AI.result: On community-level mobility data from Shenzhen, China, ODE-DynNet reduces infection cost by 88% (from 4,930 to 590) compared to a non-steady partially observable decoupled policy using raw proxies without reconstruction, and remains effective across varying transmission intensities and reporting delays.
AI.conclusion: Explicit observation modeling and mechanistic state reconstruction serve as effective preprocessing steps for learned epidemic-control policies under incomplete surveillance.

title: Revisiting Mixture Policies in Entropy-Regularized Actor-Critic

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a marginalized reparameterization (MRP) gradient estimator for mixture policies in entropy-regularized actor-critic reinforcement learning, making mixture policies practical and competitive with Gaussian policies.
AI.motivation: Although mixture policies offer greater theoretical flexibility and entropy robustness than unimodal Gaussian policies in continuous action RL, standard algorithms like SAC cannot exploit them due to the lack of a low-variance reparameterization trick.
AI.method: The authors introduce the marginalized reparameterization (MRP) estimator for mixture policies and prove it has lower variance than the standard likelihood-ratio (LR) estimator in a simplified bandit setting.
AI.result: In Gym MuJoCo, MRP mixture policies significantly outperform LR counterparts; across Gym MuJoCo, DeepMind Control Suite, MetaWorld, and MyoSuite, they match or surpass Gaussian policies without retuning Gaussian-tuned hyperparameters, and clearly outperform Gaussian policies on classic-control tasks with unshaped rewards.
AI.conclusion: The marginalized reparameterization estimator resolves the high-variance gradient bottleneck of mixture policies, turning them into a practical tool for continuous control.

title: Discovery and Spatial Characterisation of Multiple Shortcut Groups for Auditing Vision Model Bias

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a per-image spatial characterization method to discover multiple recurring shortcut groups in vision models and introduces a feature intervention that reduces subgroup performance disparities.
AI.motivation: Existing attribution-based bias auditing methods aggregate regional rankings across images before computing dataset-level maps, which can mask recurring spatial shortcut patterns present only in subsets of images.
AI.method: The authors compute per-image shortcut and task contribution maps, cluster their joint representations using K-means and non-negative matrix factorization to identify shortcut groups, and propose a combined shortcut suppression and task amplification feature intervention.
AI.result: Across CelebA, CheXpert, Waterbirds, Camelyon17, and ISIC2019 on ResNet and ViT models, the discovered groups reveal shared and distinct spatial shortcut patterns linked to subgroup error rates, while input occlusion and internal interventions show that suppressing task regions degrades performance and the combined intervention generally reduces performance disparities.
AI.conclusion: Per-image spatial characterization uncovers localized shortcut groups behind subgroup errors and enables targeted feature interventions to mitigate bias.

title: GRASP: Query-Adaptive Graph Retrieval framework with Cross-Attention Scoring and Path Sufficiency Verification for Question Answering
summary: Retrieval quality is a key factor in the reliability of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), particularly when retrieval is performed over structured knowledge graphs. Graph-based retrieval requires decisions about candidate-edge scoring, traversal termination, and the sufficiency of the retrieved evidence. We propose GRASP, a query-adaptive graph retrieval framework that jointly addresses these decisions during the retrieval process. A cross-attention scorer models fine-grained interactions between individual query tokens and candidate edges, providing query-specific signals for edge selection. A learned stopping gate conditions traversal termination on the query, traversal state, and hop depth, allowing the retrieval depth to adapt to the current retrieval state. A sufficiency classifier further evaluates the assembled path before generation and triggers re-retrieval when the evidence is predicted to be incomplete. We evaluate GRASP on three biomedical question-answering benchmarks with different graph scales and answer lengths, using biomedical question answering as a representative setting for evaluating graph-based RAG retrieval. GRASP consistently improves over the strongest learned baseline across the evaluated retrieval and generation metrics. The unsupported-claim rate is reduced by 8.9% to 13.2% across the three benchmarks, with the largest reduction on the benchmark with the longest generated answers. The retrieval gains are more pronounced under higher candidate density, while ablation results indicate that the three components provide complementary improvements.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces GRASP, a query-adaptive graph retrieval framework for RAG that jointly handles candidate-edge scoring, traversal termination, and path sufficiency verification.
AI.motivation: Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation requires accurate decisions on edge scoring, when to stop traversal, and whether retrieved evidence is sufficient, which existing methods struggle to coordinate adaptively.
AI.method: GRASP combines a cross-attention scorer modeling token-level interactions between queries and candidate edges, a learned stopping gate conditioned on query, traversal state, and hop depth, and a path sufficiency classifier that triggers re-retrieval when evidence is predicted incomplete.
AI.result: Evaluated on three biomedical QA benchmarks with varying graph scales and answer lengths, GRASP outperforms the strongest learned baseline across retrieval and generation metrics, reducing unsupported-claim rates by 8.9% to 13.2%, with larger gains under higher candidate density.
AI.conclusion: Jointly adapting edge scoring, traversal depth, and evidence verification significantly improves the reliability and groundedness of graph-based RAG.

title: Interlocking Tiling of 3D Finite Domains
summary: A K-hedral tiling of a 3D finite domain is a covering of the domain with tiles without gaps or overlaps, where each tile is congruent to one of the K distinct shapes called prototiles. To use 3D K-hedral tilings in practice, they need to satisfy two requirements. First, K should be small to reduce the fabrication cost (e.g., through reusable molds) and simplify the (dis)assembly process. Second, a K-hedral tiling result should be structurally stable, in particular via interlocking, where all the tiles are immobilized by their geometric arrangement, except the key. Since these two requirements are often in conflict, existing approaches always trade one for the other. In this work, we formulate a new tiling problem called interlocking tiling, aiming to generate 3D K-hedral tilings that satisfy the above two requirements simultaneously. Given a 3D finite domain represented as a voxel grid, our goal is to compute a small prototile set whose instances exactly tile the input domain while ensuring that the tiling result forms an interlocking assembly. To solve this challenging problem, we propose a twolevel computational approach that hierarchically decomposes the input domain into interlocking parts (domain-level partitioning) and further partitions each part into interlocking tiles (part-level partitioning). To guide the part-level partitioning, we propose a new graph representation with regular structures to facilitate the generation of tiles with identical shapes while ensuring that they are interlocking. Our approach allows generating interlocking tilings that exactly cover 3D finite domains with diverse shapes while achieving high prototile reuse. We compared our approach with state-of-the-art methods to demonstrate its superiority, and validated the practicality of our interlocking tiling results via fabricating two of them.

AI.tldr: This paper formulates the interlocking tiling problem for 3D finite domains and proposes a two-level computational approach to generate K-hedral tilings with high prototile reuse and structural interlocking.
AI.motivation: Practical 3D K-hedral tilings require both a small number of distinct prototiles K to lower fabrication costs and interlocking geometry for structural stability, two requirements that existing methods typically trade off against each other.
AI.method: Given a 3D voxel-grid domain, the method performs domain-level partitioning into interlocking parts followed by part-level partitioning into interlocking tiles, guided by a regular-structured graph representation that promotes identical tile shapes.
AI.result: Comparisons with state-of-the-art methods demonstrate superior prototile reuse and exact domain coverage across diverse 3D shapes, and physical fabrication of two interlocking tilings validates their practicality.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical interlocking decomposition with a regular graph representation enables simultaneous prototile reuse and structural stability in 3D K-hedral tilings.

title: RemeshingAgent: An Iterative Agent for Repair-Based Decimation of Generated Building Meshes
summary: Aggressively simplifying a generated high-poly building mesh to 0.5-1% of its faces confronts a hard limit. The surface looks complete, yet the mesh is topologically shattered: 10^3-10^4 connected components and non-manifold thin walls. Below a certain budget, every practical decimator "melts": it deletes parts, welds thin walls, or breaks the error tolerance. We attribute this to instance-specific pathology: which components are significant and where the cliff sits vary from mesh to mesh, so no single fixed algorithm suffices, and decimation becomes an iterative loop of cleaning, simplifying, and verifying. We present RemeshingAgent, an agent that turns this loop into a validated process. The melting follows from a triangle-budget decomposition into curvature, crease, component, and genus terms: below the component floor, no output satisfies the repair contract, and cleaning first is the theory-mandated response. At a 0.5% budget the agent stays topology-clean where QEM and vertex clustering melt, matches a commercial remesher on 20 unseen city buildings, and on the 24 training buildings a nine-participant single-workstation blind study prefers our outputs 168:48 (p = 0.0195, subject-level sign test). The trained skill deploys as retrieval replay: 11.7 seconds per mesh on CPU, with no LLM calls.

AI.tldr: This paper presents RemeshingAgent, an iterative repair-based decimation agent that simplifies generated high-poly building meshes to 0.5-1% of their faces without topological melting.
AI.motivation: Aggressively decimating generated building meshes with 10^3 to 10^4 connected components and non-manifold thin walls causes standard decimators to melt geometry, and instance-specific pathology prevents any single fixed algorithm from succeeding.
AI.method: Guided by a triangle-budget decomposition into curvature, crease, component, and genus terms, RemeshingAgent runs an iterative loop of cleaning first, simplifying, and verifying against a repair contract, deploying the trained skill as retrieval replay without LLM calls.
AI.result: At a 0.5% triangle budget, RemeshingAgent stays topology-clean where QEM and vertex clustering melt, matches a commercial remesher on 20 unseen city buildings, wins a blind user study 168:48 (p = 0.0195) on 24 training buildings, and runs in 11.7 seconds per mesh on CPU.
AI.conclusion: Framing aggressive mesh decimation as an iterative, theory-guided repair-and-verify loop enables topology-preserving simplification of complex generated buildings at low CPU cost.

title: A Self-Evolving Agent Runs Like a Gas: Describing and Predicting Its Evolution with Fluid Dynamics
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables. Submitted to AAMAS 2027 (Blue Sky Ideas Track); under review
summary: A self-evolving LLM agent improves in service by rewriting its own plugin library under a validation gate. Agent engineering is converging on exactly such agents: single systems in continuous operation, carrying populations of runtime instances (plugins, skills, tools) past the point where anyone can read the library and still predict what the system will do. Yet the run itself, the aggregate motion of that population across hundreds of edit rounds, is unstudied: no theory says whether it relaxes, oscillates, or freezes. A recent kinetic theory supplies the missing level: under four architectural properties, the plugin instances of one agent behave as identical hard spheres whose density obeys a master equation, and the theory is candid that its gate injects and drains credit, momentum is not conserved, and waves are excluded by construction. We argue the boundary is architectural; keeping the four safety theorems, we stack conservation axioms on top. A closed-credit ledger makes credit a collision invariant and unlocks acoustic waves at a measurable, engineerable speed; a zero-sum projection gate conserves centroid momentum unconditionally, for any proposal stream. Both layers are proven and executed: the axis total is conserved to the digit over 66 interventions under a live gate, and the pre-registered decisive probe returns the theory's directional verdict: linear wavefronts where the ledger holds, dissipation where it does not, replicated across two population sizes. For agents that must never stop, the gas description is not a metaphor: it is the measurement interface through which their future becomes readable.

AI.tldr: This paper extends kinetic theory for self-evolving LLM agents with a closed-credit ledger and zero-sum projection gate, enabling conserved momentum and measurable acoustic waves in plugin populations.
AI.motivation: Self-evolving agents that rewrite their own plugin libraries under validation gates lack a macro-level theory predicting whether their runtime instance populations relax, oscillate, or freeze across hundreds of edit rounds.
AI.method: Building on a hard-sphere master-equation kinetic theory, the authors add a closed-credit ledger making credit a collision invariant and a zero-sum projection gate that unconditionally conserves centroid momentum while preserving four safety theorems.
AI.result: Over 66 interventions under a live gate, the axis total is conserved to the digit, and a pre-registered probe confirms linear wavefronts when the ledger holds and dissipation when it does not across two population sizes.
AI.conclusion: Conservation axioms turn fluid dynamics into a quantitative measurement interface for predicting the long-run behavior of continuously self-evolving agents.

title: One Code per Material: Neural Representation and Generation of Measured BTFs
summary: Measured bidirectional texture functions (BTFs) capture the full appearance of real materials--including parallax, self-shadowing and inter-reflections that analytic SVBRDFs cannot express--but each measurement is billions of values, and every new material requires a new capture. Existing neural BTF representations encode each material as large per-texel latent maps rather than as a point in a shared space from which new materials could be sampled. We present neural representations of measured BTFs at two operating points. A per-material coordinate network outperforms the recent neural BTF of Xia et al. at matched size (+3.2 dB PSNR) and all prior baselines on every metric. A compact model represents each material by a single 256-dimensional code that conditions a shared decoder; it exceeds the PSNR (+1.2 dB) and colour accuracy of the per-texel latent maps of Rainer et al. with 256 numbers per material instead of millions, and one decoder shared by all materials. Because each material is a single point in this code space, measured BTFs can be sampled: a class-conditional flow over the codes, trained on the 84 materials enlarged with colourways and hue rotations, generates materials that render and relight as full BTFs.

AI.tldr: This paper presents two neural representations for measured bidirectional texture functions (BTFs), including a compact 256-dimensional single-code-per-material model that enables generative BTF sampling.
AI.motivation: Measured BTFs capture rich material appearance but require billions of values per material, while existing neural BTFs use large per-texel latent maps that prevent sampling new materials from a shared space.
AI.method: The authors propose a per-material coordinate network and a compact shared-decoder model encoding each material as a single 256-dimensional code, then train a class-conditional flow over codes from 84 augmented materials to generate new BTFs.
AI.result: The per-material coordinate network outperforms Xia et al. by +3.2 dB PSNR at matched size, while the 256-dimensional code model beats Rainer et al.'s per-texel latent maps by +1.2 dB PSNR and higher colour accuracy using one shared decoder.
AI.conclusion: Representing each measured BTF as a single compact code in a shared latent space both improves compression and accuracy and enables generative synthesis of relightable materials.

title: Real-world Polarimetric Environment Map Dataset
comment: Published in SIGGRAPH Asia 2026 Conference Papers
summary: Environment maps are a standard representation of illumination, enabling realistic image-based lighting in modern rendering systems. However, existing environment maps typically encode only RGB radiance, omitting polarization, an intrinsic property of light that is imperceptible to the human eye but informative about surface shape and material properties. This omission precludes the physically accurate simulation of polarized light transport under in-the-wild illumination conditions, heavily limiting the development and evaluation of robust polarization-based scene reconstruction and understanding methods. We address this gap by introducing a real-world polarimetric environment map dataset, each providing a full-sphere panorama with per-pixel high-dynamic-range RGB Stokes vectors. To acquire the dataset, we design and calibrate a dedicated imaging system and develop a polarization-aware panorama-stitching pipeline. In particular, we introduce a frame-field representation for perspective cameras, together with singularity-aware blending, to enable smooth polarimetric panorama stitching without singularity artifacts. Using this system, we capture 100 polarimetric environment maps across diverse real-world scenes. We further develop a custom rendering plugin and demonstrate close agreement between real and rendered observations. Finally, we analyze the polarization state of the sky across different times and weather conditions, and demonstrate its practical impact on a downstream shape-from-polarization task.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a real-world dataset of 100 full-sphere HDR polarimetric environment maps along with a dedicated imaging system, singularity-aware stitching pipeline, and rendering plugin.
AI.motivation: Standard RGB environment maps omit polarization, preventing physically accurate simulation of polarized light transport under in-the-wild illumination and limiting polarization-based scene reconstruction research.
AI.method: The authors build and calibrate a polarimetric imaging system and develop a polarization-aware panorama-stitching pipeline using a perspective camera frame-field representation and singularity-aware blending to capture per-pixel HDR RGB Stokes vectors.
AI.result: They capture 100 diverse real-world polarimetric environment maps, demonstrate close agreement between real and rendered observations via a custom rendering plugin, analyze sky polarization across times and weather, and show practical impact on shape-from-polarization.
AI.conclusion: Providing calibrated real-world polarimetric environment maps and rendering tools removes a key data bottleneck for polarized light transport simulation and shape-from-polarization.

title: ReMoVe: Refining a Video Model's Own Motion for Coherent Human Video Generation
summary: Video generation models have become increasingly capable of synthesizing realistic human motion, yet they often lose track of the very structure that makes the motion plausible. As generated human motion becomes more complex, videos can suffer from progressive body deformation and appearance drift across frames. Existing motion-controlled methods use explicit representations to stabilize generation, but typically rely on pre-defined motion sequences as references. This raises a fundamental question: if the base generator already produces a usable coarse motion, why replace it with an external one? ReMoVe answers this question by treating the coarse output as a motion hypothesis rather than a final result. ReMoVe recovers and refines the underlying motion, then renders the refined motion as 3D mesh and transfers facial appearance onto it, thereby improving motion accuracy and identity consistency. We further derive depth from the same 3D scene and camera trajectory to impose scene-level spatial consistency beyond the mesh. By jointly conditioning video generation models on mesh and depth, ReMoVe synthesizes high-quality motion videos with controllable camera trajectories and enhanced spatio-temporal consistency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ReMoVe improves human structural stability, appearance consistency, temporal coherence, and motion-following fidelity, while retaining the base generator's motion prior and offering accurate camera control.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes ReMoVe, a framework that refines a video generator's own coarse human motion into a 3D mesh and depth conditioning signal to synthesize coherent human videos with controllable cameras.
AI.motivation: Video generation models often suffer from body deformation and appearance drift during complex human motion, while existing motion-controlled methods rely on external pre-defined motion references rather than leveraging the base generator's own motion prior.
AI.method: ReMoVe treats the base generator's coarse output as a motion hypothesis, recovers and refines the 3D human motion into a mesh, transfers facial appearance onto it, derives scene depth along the camera trajectory, and jointly conditions video generation on mesh and depth.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show that ReMoVe improves human structural stability, appearance consistency, temporal coherence, and motion-following fidelity while preserving the base generator's motion prior and enabling accurate camera control.
AI.conclusion: Refining a video model's own coarse motion into 3D mesh and depth conditions provides an effective self-consistent path to coherent, camera-controllable human video generation.

title: ImpedanceMimic: Learned Impedance as Action Space for Force-Accurate Motion Imitation
comment: 39 pages, 13 figures, 28 tables. Project page: this https URL
summary: Recovering the forces behind a motion is ill-posed: different controllers can reproduce the same movement while generating different contact forces. Physics-based motion imitation resolves this ambiguity through simulation, but relies on fixed-gain proportional-derivative (PD) control. We show that fixed gains impose a trade-off between motion and force tracking, as contact and swing place conflicting demands on joint stiffness and damping. We introduce ImpedanceMimic, a reinforcement-learning policy that modulates per-joint stiffness, damping, and position setpoints from motion and force measurements, but requires only motion at inference. Across 129 participants and six activities, ImpedanceMimic outperforms matched fixed-gain PD under every integration scheme, direct-torque, muscle-actuated and existing imitation controllers in kinematic and force fidelity, approaching a dedicated motion-to-force regressor. By expressing gains as multiples of inertia-scaled priors, a single policy controls subject-specific biomechanical models without explicit anthropometric input and transfers zero-shot to unseen humans and a humanoid robot. The learned impedance forms a low-dimensional representation of motor state, shared across bodies, that generalizes to withheld activities: stiffness scales with load, and damping anticipates unloading.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces ImpedanceMimic, an RL policy that uses learned per-joint impedance as its action space to achieve force-accurate, zero-shot transferable physics-based motion imitation.
AI.motivation: Recovering contact forces from motion via physics-based imitation is ill-posed under fixed-gain PD control, which forces a trade-off between motion and force tracking because contact and swing require conflicting joint stiffness and damping.
AI.method: ImpedanceMimic trains an RL policy to modulate per-joint stiffness, damping, and position setpoints as multiples of inertia-scaled priors using motion and force measurements during training, while requiring only motion at inference.
AI.result: Across 129 participants and six activities, ImpedanceMimic outperforms fixed-gain PD, direct-torque, muscle-actuated, and existing imitation controllers in kinematic and force fidelity, approaching a dedicated motion-to-force regressor and transferring zero-shot to unseen humans and a humanoid robot.
AI.conclusion: Expressing control actions as inertia-scaled learned impedance resolves the motion-force trade-off and yields a shared motor-state representation that generalizes across bodies and activities.

title: Prepare Lighter and Faster for Open-Vocabulary Queries: A Query-Wise 3D Segmenter for Gaussian Splatting
summary: Open-vocabulary 3D understanding aims to localize and segment arbitrary objects beyond predefined categories. However, existing approaches based on Gaussian Splatting often rely on expensive preprocessing and lengthy training, limiting their applicability when fast and lightweight solutions are desired. We propose a lightweight, training-free framework for query-driven 3D instance segmentation on Gaussian Splatting. Instead of conventional mask-wise CLIP embeddings, we use dense pixel-level CLIP features to preserve fine-grained semantic information and enable flexible text-driven localization without relying on predefined instance proposals. Given a text query, we identify a high-quality target region in a carefully selected pivot view and propagate it across views using a video segmentor, providing consistent and comprehensive coverage of the target instance. We then lift the resulting 2D tracklets to 3D Gaussians through a novel visibility voting strategy, yielding accurate 3D segmentation masks with clean object boundaries. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on LERF-OVS, ScanNet, and ScanNet++, competitive results on 3D-OVS, and significant speedups over existing open-vocabulary 3D segmentation methods. These results highlight the effectiveness of our framework for efficient open-vocabulary 3D understanding without per-scene training.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a lightweight, training-free framework for query-wise open-vocabulary 3D instance segmentation on Gaussian Splatting using dense pixel-level CLIP features and cross-view propagation.
AI.motivation: Existing open-vocabulary 3D segmentation methods for Gaussian Splatting typically require expensive preprocessing and lengthy per-scene training, limiting fast and lightweight deployment.
AI.method: Given a text query, the method uses dense pixel-level CLIP features to locate a target region in a selected pivot view, propagates it across views with a video segmentor, and lifts the 2D tracklets to 3D Gaussians via a visibility voting strategy.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on LERF-OVS, ScanNet, and ScanNet++, competitive results on 3D-OVS, and significant speedups over existing open-vocabulary 3D segmentation methods without per-scene training.
AI.conclusion: Combining dense pixel-level CLIP localization, video segmentation propagation, and visibility voting enables fast, accurate, training-free open-vocabulary 3D segmentation on Gaussian Splatting.

title: A Line is Not Just a Line: Visualizing Harmonious Complex Line Sets
summary: Line is a foundational building block in visual design for traditional media and computer graphics. Controlled variation in line quality can be used to define form, create abstractions, distinguish categories, control affect, and more. Yet, when it comes to computer graphics visualizations of science, particularly those built upon 3D computer graphics, too often a line is just a line. This portfolio presents a series of visual design studies and lessons learned that explore the diverse character of line that might be useful for 3D visualizations. The imagery begins to show how more sophisticated use of this powerful visual building block could increase the clarity of data visualizations while also bringing a human, handcrafted aesthetic that reinforces the people and impacts behind scientific climate data.

AI.tldr: This portfolio presents visual design studies exploring how controlled variations in line quality can improve clarity and human resonance in 3D scientific visualizations.
AI.motivation: While traditional media use varied line quality to convey form, categories, and affect, 3D computer graphics visualizations of scientific data typically render lines uniformly without exploiting their expressive potential.
AI.method: The author conducts a series of visual design studies and distills lessons on applying diverse line characteristics within 3D scientific visualizations, particularly for climate data.
AI.result: The resulting imagery illustrates how sophisticated line variation can increase visual clarity in complex 3D data visualizations while introducing a handcrafted aesthetic that highlights the human impact behind climate science.
AI.conclusion: Treating line quality as an intentional design variable offers a promising way to make 3D scientific visualizations both clearer and more engaging.

title: From XR Sketches to CAD: Preserving Design Intent with AI
comment: Vision paper (6 pages, 1 figure) submitted to the Workshop on AI-Augmented 3D Sketching in Extended Reality (ACE-XR) at IEEE AIxVR 2027
summary: Extended reality (XR) allows designers to sketch shapes directly in 3D, but converting these sketches into editable, feature-based CAD requires interpreting their intent. A sketch may contain drawing errors, intended features, and design choices that remain open. Correcting every irregularity risks erasing intended features, while automatic completion may impose choices the designer has not made. We argue that AI should add precision without overriding design intent, considering both the resulting shape and how the CAD model behaves during later edits. To guide this process, we propose a conceptual framework that distinguishes errors from intentions in individual sketch properties and relates them to correction, preservation, and exploration in editable CAD. We also outline five research directions for sketch interpretation, CAD construction, and evaluation, with testable hypotheses for selected questions.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a conceptual framework and research agenda for using AI to convert 3D XR sketches into editable, feature-based CAD models while preserving designer intent.
AI.motivation: Turning freehand 3D XR sketches into editable CAD models is difficult because aggressive error correction can erase intended features, whereas automatic completion can impose unmade design choices.
AI.method: The authors introduce a conceptual framework that separates drawing errors from intended features and open design choices at the property level, mapping them to correction, preservation, and exploration in editable CAD, alongside five research directions and testable hypotheses.
AI.result: The paper delivers a structured taxonomy of sketch-to-CAD intent preservation and formulates concrete research questions and hypotheses for sketch interpretation, CAD construction, and evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Framing AI-assisted XR-to-CAD conversion around distinguishing errors from intent and open choices provides a principled foundation for future editable 3D design tools.

title: CiGS: Conduction in Gaussian Splats for Interior Temperature Field from Thermal Images
summary: We present a method for inferring the interior temperature distribution of a solid object from registered multi-view visible-spectrum and thermal images, even when the thermal views cover only part of its surface. We formulate steady-state heat conduction as a Laplace boundary value problem and solve it with a direct boundary integral equation discretized over a point cloud: a Gaussian reconstruction of the visible-spectrum images supplies the boundary geometry, and the thermal images supply the boundary data. We do not build surface or volume meshes at any stage in our method. Instead, we sample collocation points from rendered depth without the pixels at depth discontinuities, and use a density subtraction that keeps the interior evaluation accurate up to the surface. The whole chain is differentiable, and we use it to recover the pose and depth of heating pipes, insulation defects, and the shape of cracks from thermal images. We validate our method through experiments on boundary value problems with Dirichlet-only and mixed Dirichlet and Robin boundaries, using synthetic and real captured data on scenes with challenging topology. These experiments show that our method matches analytical solutions and has better accuracy than FEM solvers.

AI.tldr: This paper presents CiGS, a differentiable mesh-free method that infers the interior temperature field of a solid object from registered multi-view visible and partial thermal images.
AI.motivation: Recovering interior temperature distributions from partial surface thermal views is challenging, and conventional finite element solvers require building surface or volume meshes.
AI.method: CiGS formulates steady-state heat conduction as a Laplace boundary value problem solved via a direct boundary integral equation discretized over a point cloud, using Gaussian reconstruction of visible images for geometry, thermal images for boundary data, depth-sampled collocation points, and density subtraction.
AI.result: On synthetic and real captured scenes with Dirichlet-only and mixed Dirichlet-Robin boundaries and challenging topology, CiGS matches analytical solutions, outperforms FEM solvers in accuracy, and recovers heating pipe poses, insulation defects, and crack shapes.
AI.conclusion: Discretizing differentiable boundary integral equations directly on Gaussian-splat point clouds enables accurate, mesh-free inverse thermal reconstruction of solid interiors.

title: Pointillist Maize: 3D Reconstruction of Field-Grown Maize Using RGB UAV Imagery
comment: 26 pages, 8 figures, submitted to Frontiers in Plant Science
summary: Three-dimensional reconstruction can extend field phenotyping to individual maize organs, but thin, flexible, occluding structures and plant movement complicate reconstruction. We evaluated whether consumer-grade UAV RGB video processed with Structure from Motion and multi-view stereo could recover recognizable field-grown maize structures, and examined the effects of acquisition trajectories and frame sampling. COLMAP reconstructions preserved recognizable leaves, stems, tassel branches, ears, silks, and brace roots. For an equal-frame comparison, we reconstructed one plant from two sets of 295 frames from the same video: a single orbit sampled at 5 frames/second and three orbits at different altitudes (ribbon skirt) sampled at 2 frames/second. After ground removal, the reconstructions contained 520,601 and 375,318 points, respectively. The single orbit yielded greater point concentration within plant structures and fewer visible gaps, while the ribbon skirt yielded fewer scattered points and slightly lower proportions of isolated points. In densely planted nursery rows, visible voids occupied 17.57% of the rendered scene with one orbit at 1 frame/second, decreasing to 5.07% with additional serpentine passes and 2.68% when the original orbit was sampled at 3 frames/second. Additional observations also increased point dispersion associated with plant movement. A curlicue trajectory tested in a different field in 2024 produced distinguishable individual plants without visible duplicated structures, although substantial voids remained, mainly on the soil surface. These results demonstrate the feasibility of recovering recognizable maize organs from consumer UAV imagery and reveal trade-offs between acquisition strategies, reconstruction completeness, and point dispersion. Independent geometric validation is still needed before quantitative phenotyping.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates consumer-grade UAV RGB video with SfM and multi-view stereo for 3D reconstruction of field-grown maize, analyzing how flight trajectories and frame sampling affect completeness and point dispersion.
AI.motivation: Extending 3D field phenotyping to individual maize organs is hindered by thin, flexible, occluding plant structures and wind-induced plant movement.
AI.method: The authors process consumer UAV RGB videos using COLMAP SfM/MVS under different trajectories (single orbit, multi-altitude ribbon skirt, serpentine passes, curlicue) and frame sampling rates (1 to 5 fps), comparing point counts, visible voids, and point dispersion.
AI.result: COLMAP recovers recognizable leaves, stems, tassels, ears, silks, and brace roots; at 295 frames, single-orbit 5 fps yields 520,601 points with fewer gaps while 2 fps ribbon skirt yields 375,318 points with fewer scattered points, and nursery-row voids drop from 17.57% (1 fps) to 5.07% (serpentine) and 2.68% (3 fps).
AI.conclusion: Consumer UAV RGB imagery can reconstruct detailed maize organs, though acquisition strategies trade off completeness against movement-induced dispersion and still require independent geometric validation before quantitative phenotyping.

title: A Gaussian Primitive Data Management Framework for Efficient 3DGS Trajectory Rendering
summary: Trajectory rendering, which renders novel views of a reconstructed 3D scene along a camera path, is a core operation in digital twins and autonomous inspection. Structured 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) renders a single view in real time by decoding sparse anchors into Gaussians on demand, but it renders a trajectory view by view: every view projects all anchors to select them, re-decodes anchors already requested by neighboring views, and runs all steps on the GPU while the CPU idles. We treat this as a spatial data management problem, where anchors are spatial objects, views are range queries, and decoded Gaussians are shared derived data, and propose GDM-GS, which removes redundancy at three levels. Within a view, an anchor index and an occluder index answer each view as a holed-frustum range query, so out-of-view and provably hidden anchors are never decoded. Across views, shared materialization decodes each requested anchor once per group of consecutive views while preserving each view's selection. Across processors, a hybrid pipeline balances selections between the CPU and the GPU before grouped decoding under bounded memory. Experiments on large-scale public scenes show that GDM-GS substantially reduces trajectory rendering latency while preserving image quality.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces GDM-GS, a three-level spatial data management framework that accelerates 3D Gaussian Splatting trajectory rendering without sacrificing image quality.
AI.motivation: Structured 3DGS renders trajectories inefficiently view by view, repeatedly projecting all anchors, re-decoding anchors shared across neighboring views, and leaving the CPU idle while the GPU handles all work.
AI.method: GDM-GS models trajectory rendering as spatial data management with holed-frustum range queries using anchor and occluder indices within views, shared anchor materialization across consecutive views, and a hybrid CPU-GPU selection pipeline under bounded memory.
AI.result: Experiments on large-scale public scenes demonstrate that GDM-GS substantially reduces trajectory rendering latency while preserving rendered image quality.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting spatial indexing, cross-view anchor reuse, and hybrid CPU-GPU execution removes key redundancies in structured 3DGS trajectory rendering.

title: KuroshioVis: Hypothesis-Driven Discovery of Mesoscale Air-Sea Interaction through Coarse-to-Fine Exploration
summary: Mesoscale air-sea interaction occurs throughout strong sea surface temperature fronts such as the the Kuroshio Extension, but its strength is highly non-uniform and can be resolved only in kilometre-scale coupled simulations. The response of any single eddy is weak relative to synoptic variability, so evidence supporting a hypothesis of systematic air-sea coupling must be accumulated across many eddies rather than inferred from individual cases. We present KuroshioVis, a hypothesis-driven, coarse-to-fine visual analytics workflow. The coarse stage extracts and aligns mesoscale eddies into composite representations of their air-sea responses, and provides a global view for exploration. The fine stage investigates these responses through three coordinated views: the composite in terface view, the cross-interface flow view, and the evidence matrix view. These coordinated views support air-sea coupling analysis from surface patterns to cross-interface dynamics and quantitative statistical evidence. We demonstrate the workflow using the coupled C1440-LLC2160 simulation of the 2026 SciVis Contest.

AI.tldr: This paper presents KuroshioVis, a hypothesis-driven, coarse-to-fine visual analytics workflow for discovering systematic mesoscale air-sea interactions across many eddies in kilometre-scale coupled simulations.
AI.motivation: Because individual mesoscale eddies exhibit weak air-sea responses relative to synoptic variability, evidence for systematic air-sea coupling must be aggregated across many eddies rather than drawn from isolated cases.
AI.method: KuroshioVis uses a coarse stage to extract and align mesoscale eddies into composite representations for global exploration, followed by a fine stage with three coordinated views (composite interface, cross-interface flow, and evidence matrix) linking surface patterns, cross-interface dynamics, and statistical evidence.
AI.result: The workflow is demonstrated on the coupled C1440-LLC2160 simulation from the 2026 SciVis Contest, enabling exploration of air-sea coupling in the Kuroshio Extension.
AI.conclusion: Combining eddy compositing with coordinated multi-view statistical analysis supports hypothesis-driven discovery of weak but systematic mesoscale air-sea interactions.

title: Ensemble Bounds for Pairwise Dissimilar Decomposition of Deterministic Datasets
comment: Accepted for publication in Springer Proceedings in Mathematics and Statistics, QEDS conference, Ranchi, India
summary: In this paper, we study reduced similarity decompositions of \emph{deterministic} datasets using redundancy graphs and obtain \emph{ensemble} bounds for the minimum size of such constrained decomposition. We consider batch decompositions that reduce similarity \emph{across} batches and use the Lovász local lemma to obtain bounds for the minimum size of a decomposition with a given pairwise dissimilarity. We then consider unique batch decomposition with a given relaxation parameter and obtain upper and lower ensemble bounds for the minimum size. Throughout, we use Binomial random graphs to obtain the desired ensemble bounds, by conditioning on the number of similar \emph{pairs} of data points.

AI.tldr: This paper derives ensemble upper and lower bounds on the minimum size of pairwise dissimilar batch decompositions of deterministic datasets using redundancy and Binomial random graphs.
AI.motivation: Reducing similarity across batches in deterministic datasets requires understanding the minimum achievable decomposition size under pairwise dissimilarity constraints.
AI.method: The authors model dataset similarity via redundancy graphs, apply the Lovasz local lemma to bound batch decompositions with given pairwise dissimilarity, and analyze unique batch decompositions with relaxation parameters by conditioning Binomial random graphs on the number of similar pairs.
AI.result: The paper establishes theoretical ensemble upper and lower bounds for the minimum size of both pairwise dissimilar batch decompositions and relaxed unique batch decompositions.
AI.conclusion: Conditioning Binomial random graphs on similar-pair counts provides a rigorous framework for bounding the size of dissimilarity-constrained dataset decompositions.

title: Domino: Joint Unmasking via First-order Markov Chain for Few-Step Masked Diffusion
summary: Masked diffusion models generate a sequence by revealing masked positions over many denoising steps. A few-step sampler has to reveal many positions at once, but the standard reverse kernel draws them independently and primarily ignores the conditional dependence between tokens revealed in the same step. We propose a novel framework called Domino, which models this dependence with a first-order Markov chain over the revealed positions, given the current state. The first revealed position keeps the posterior of a pre-trained masked diffusion model (MDM), and each subsequent position follows a transition given the token of its predecessor. Notably, the resulting step is normalized by construction, contains the factorized step in MDMs as a special case, and has a likelihood in closed form. We implement the Domino transitions via a lightweight module on the hidden states of a pre-trained MDM denoiser with only 2.6% parameter overhead and train by keeping the MDM denoiser frozen. Our extensive evaluations across text, molecules, and images show that Domino lowers the few-step generative perplexity of MDMs by a factor of 1.7 to 3.8 on One Billion Word (LM1B), WikiText-103, and OpenWebText at nearly unchanged sample entropy. It also raises the validity of few-step molecule samples by 1.5x. The source code is available at: this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Domino, a lightweight first-order Markov chain framework that models conditional dependencies among tokens unmasked simultaneously in few-step masked diffusion models.
AI.motivation: Few-step masked diffusion samplers must unmask many tokens in parallel per step, but standard factorized reverse kernels sample them independently and ignore conditional dependencies among co-revealed tokens.
AI.method: Domino models co-revealed positions as a first-order Markov chain given the current state, keeping the pre-trained MDM posterior for the first token and adding a lightweight transition module (2.6% parameter overhead) trained on hidden states with the MDM denoiser frozen.
AI.result: Across text, molecules, and images, Domino reduces few-step generative perplexity by 1.7x to 3.8x on LM1B, WikiText-103, and OpenWebText at nearly unchanged sample entropy, and increases few-step molecule validity by 1.5x.
AI.conclusion: Adding a lightweight, normalized Markov transition module over parallel unmasked tokens substantially improves few-step masked diffusion quality with minimal parameter overhead.

title: Trajectory-Based Bayesian Discovery of a Host-Pathogen Model from Quasi-Steady-State Observations
summary: System identification of nonlinear dynamical systems becomes challenging when the measured data come from a nearly settled state. We study this situation in the case of a bistable host-pathogen interaction model with a cubic term, whose seven true mechanisms are hidden among twenty candidate terms. The data are from one noise-free trajectory on a quasi-steady-state observed window and the initial state. In this situation, classical sparse identification approaches fail to identify the correct mechanisms as the candidate library becomes ill-conditioned along the quasi-steady-state trajectory. To address this, we propose an alternative approach in which sparse Bayesian learning and $\ell_{0}$ iterative hard thresholding with pursuit provide a good start, and a two-swap climb on the Bayesian evidence of the candidate ODE solutions recovers the true model. Our results show successful model recovery, i.e., correct identification of its support and accurate estimation of its coefficients, as validated by exhaustive scoring.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Bayesian system identification method combining sparse Bayesian learning, l0 iterative hard thresholding, and a two-swap Bayesian evidence climb to recover a host-pathogen ODE model from quasi-steady-state data.
AI.motivation: Classical sparse identification fails to recover nonlinear dynamical systems when observations come from a nearly settled quasi-steady-state trajectory, because the candidate term library becomes severely ill-conditioned.
AI.method: Applied to a bistable host-pathogen model with seven true terms among twenty candidates using one noise-free trajectory and its initial state, the method initializes with sparse Bayesian learning and l0 iterative hard thresholding with pursuit, then performs a two-swap climb on ODE Bayesian evidence.
AI.result: Exhaustive scoring validates that the proposed approach successfully recovers the exact model support and accurately estimates its coefficients where classical sparse identification fails.
AI.conclusion: Combining sparsity-promoting initialization with Bayesian evidence optimization over candidate ODE solutions overcomes ill-conditioning in quasi-steady-state system identification.

title: Taking Band-Limited Maximum Likelihood to High Dimensions: Linear Memory, the Parametric Rate, and a Self-Tuning Cut-off
summary: Band-limited maximum likelihood (BLML) estimates a density as the square of a band-limited function. The estimate is non-negative, and when the square root of the true density is band-limited its error falls at the parametric rate $n^{-1}$. Its algorithm bins the data, which is fast only in one or two dimensions: from three on every point has its own bin, the kernel system is dense, and memory grows as $n^2$, 40 GB at $10^5$ points. Whether the rate survives in higher dimension, where kernel estimators slow down, had not been tested. We study dense data, densities that fill their space, not data near a low-dimensional manifold. We show that the binned equations are the stationarity condition of a strictly convex objective and minimise it by block coordinate descent without forming the kernel matrix: memory is linear in $n$, a sweep costs $O(n^2 d)$ and a fit takes about ten, and one A100 GPU fits $10^6$ points in eight dimensions in about ten minutes. On band-limited truths the error then decays as $n^{-1}$ in every dimension we tested, up to eight, while the slopes of kernel estimators flatten from -0.67 to -0.28, and it is 2 to 18 times lower than a neural spline flow's. A streaming fit learns the cut-off, BLML's only tuning parameter, from analytic gradients of the held-out likelihood, for about the cost of one more fit. On real data BLML is the strongest nonparametric estimator we tested: it leads kernel and nearest-neighbour estimators on electricity prices by 0.27 to 0.47 nats per hour, and a tuned kernel estimator on the full POWER and GAS benchmarks by 0.39 and 1.58 nats per point, placing it between early and recent normalizing flows. It loses on densities with a kink.

AI.tldr: This paper scales band-limited maximum likelihood (BLML) density estimation to eight dimensions with linear memory via block coordinate descent, achieving the parametric n^-1 rate on band-limited truths and strong real-data performance.
AI.motivation: BLML achieves the fast n^-1 error rate for band-limited square-root densities, but its binning algorithm requires O(n^2) memory (40 GB at 10^5 points) and had not been tested beyond two dimensions.
AI.method: The authors show the binned equations are the stationarity condition of a strictly convex objective, solve it via block coordinate descent without forming the kernel matrix (linear memory, O(n^2 d) per sweep), and learn the cut-off parameter from analytic gradients of held-out likelihood.
AI.result: On one A100 GPU, BLML fits 10^6 points in 8D in ~10 minutes, maintains n^-1 error decay up to 8D (2-18x lower error than neural spline flows), and outperforms kernel and k-NN estimators on electricity prices (0.27-0.47 nats/h) and POWER/GAS benchmarks (0.39 and 1.58 nats/point), losing only on densities with kinks.
AI.conclusion: Matrix-free block coordinate descent makes BLML practical in higher dimensions, delivering parametric convergence rates on smooth band-limited densities and competitive nonparametric performance on real data.

title: High-dimensional limit theorems for adaptive variants of SGD I: Ballistic limits
summary: We develop the high-dimensional effective dynamics for adaptive, momentum-based variants of Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD). These effective dynamics are given by a Markov process. They key observation is that the non-Markovianity in the algorithm due to the exponential moving average and preconditioning can be treated using the method of averaging. Our approach applies to a broad class of algorithms including to Adaptive momentum estimation (ADAM), Momentum orthogonalized by Newton-Schultz (MUON), and its variants. It also applies to a broad class of learning tasks, such at tensor PCA, Gaussian projective models, teacher-student networks, and a multi-layer neural network trained on the XOR problem using a hybrid of MUON and ADAM as commonly done in practice. We demonstrate how to this technique can give precise, quantitative comparisons between algorithms. In particular, we find interesting phenomena, such as the cross-over phenomenon where online SGD has better generalization than ADAM early in training until the learning curves cross and ADAM dominates. Furthermore, we prove a version of the Edge of Stability phenomenon. In particular, we introduce an analogue of the infinity Laplacian that sharply characterizes the Edge of Stability.

AI.tldr: This paper derives high-dimensional Markovian effective dynamics for adaptive momentum-based SGD variants such as ADAM and MUON using the method of averaging, and characterizes crossover and Edge of Stability phenomena.
AI.motivation: Understanding and comparing adaptive, momentum-based optimizers in high dimensions is difficult because exponential moving averages and preconditioning introduce non-Markovian dynamics.
AI.method: Using the method of averaging, the authors derive Markovian ballistic limit dynamics for a broad class of adaptive algorithms (including ADAM, MUON, and hybrids) across tasks such as tensor PCA, Gaussian projective models, teacher-student networks, and XOR MLPs.
AI.result: The analysis yields quantitative algorithm comparisons, reveals a generalization crossover where online SGD initially beats ADAM before ADAM dominates, and proves an Edge of Stability theorem characterized by an analogue of the infinity Laplacian.
AI.conclusion: Averaging-based ballistic limits provide a unified analytical tool for comparing adaptive optimizers and explaining training dynamics like generalization crossovers and the Edge of Stability.

title: Generalization Bounds for Neural Networks with Sparse Connectivity
summary: Empirical evidence suggests that large neural networks rarely make effective use of all available parameters, with learned solutions exhibiting pronounced sparsity. Despite this ubiquity, existing generalization theory only partially explains how such sparsity influences statistical performance. In this paper, we derive non-asymptotic generalization gap bounds for deep neural networks whose layer-wise weight matrices are restricted by $\ell_p$ quasi-norm ($0<p\leq 1$) constraints. Our analysis gives rise to a novel result that interpolates between classical norm-based generalization guarantees and parameter-counting bounds. Remarkably, in the extreme sparsity limit as the quasi-norm order $p$ approaches zero, our analysis reveals a transition to a square-root dependence on the number of \emph{active} (non-zero) parameters, resulting in bounds that are strictly tighter than existing parameter-counting approaches. Experiments demonstrate that our bounds exhibit a milder dependence on initial architectural choice at the over-parametrization regime, effectively capturing the generalization benefit of the sparsity arising from training on natural data.

AI.tldr: This paper derives non-asymptotic generalization gap bounds for deep neural networks with layer-wise l_p quasi-norm (0 < p <= 1) weight constraints, bridging norm-based and parameter-counting bounds.
AI.motivation: Empirical neural networks often learn highly sparse solutions, yet existing generalization theory does not fully explain how this sparsity improves statistical performance in over-parameterized regimes.
AI.method: The authors establish non-asymptotic generalization bounds for deep networks whose layer-wise weight matrices satisfy l_p quasi-norm constraints for 0 < p <= 1, and analyze the extreme sparsity limit as p approaches zero.
AI.result: As p approaches zero, the bound transitions to a square-root dependence on the number of active (non-zero) parameters, becoming strictly tighter than existing parameter-counting bounds, and experiments confirm milder dependence on initial architecture size.
AI.conclusion: Quasi-norm generalization bounds mathematically capture the statistical benefit of learned weight sparsity and interpolate smoothly between norm-based and active-parameter complexity measures.

title: Geometric Stability and Sample Complexity for Compositional Function Priors
comment: 25 pages. An extended abstract was accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Symmetry and Geometry in Neural Representations (NeurReps), non-archival. Ancillary file: companion document with extended proofs and examples
summary: We study when compositional structure yields dimension reduction in supervised learning. We frame learning as empirical risk minimization with a function-space prior: a regularization functional selects a subset of functions with favorable approximation and metric entropy. The models are compositions $f(x)=g(Ax+\Delta h(x))$, where $A\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times d}$ is a linear base map, $\Delta h$ is a nonlinear correction, and $g$ is an outer function; that is, $f$ is an arbitrary smooth function of a $k$-dimensional representation of the input that is linear up to a correction. We prove covering-number bounds showing that the statistical complexity of this class interpolates between an intrinsic regime, parametric in the $kd$ entries of the linear map and nonparametric only in the representation dimension $k$, and an ambient $d$-dimensional nonparametric rate; the interpolation is controlled by the correction size $\varepsilon=\|\Delta h\|$. We then connect $\varepsilon$ to data geometry. If the data lie in a small tube around a $k$-dimensional manifold and the regression target depends on the input only through its nearest point on that manifold, then locally the target factorizes exactly as $g(Ax+\Delta h(x))$ with $A$ a tangent chart and a correction whose Sobolev norm scales linearly with curvature at the localization scale. Patching such local models over an atlas gives a finite-sample excess-risk bound for a least-squares estimator over a finite net of local models, whose ambient term vanishes with curvature. For a one-dimensional model problem we also prove a converse: on curved data, every affine compositional predictor faces an error floor unless its correction budget scales with curvature, while the matching curved model class attains the intrinsic rate. The correction size $\varepsilon$ is thus the effective-dimension parameter linking curvature to statistical complexity.

AI.tldr: This paper proves covering-number and excess-risk bounds for compositional function priors f(x) = g(Ax + Delta h(x)), showing how correction size links manifold curvature to effective statistical dimension.
AI.motivation: Explaining when compositional structure yields dimension reduction in supervised learning requires connecting function-space priors to the underlying geometry and curvature of data manifolds.
AI.method: The authors analyze empirical risk minimization over compositions of a linear map A, nonlinear correction Delta h, and outer function g, proving covering-number bounds, local manifold-chart factorizations, finite-sample excess-risk bounds, and a 1D lower-bound converse.
AI.result: Statistical complexity interpolates between a k-dimensional intrinsic nonparametric rate (plus kd linear parameters) and an ambient d-dimensional rate controlled by ||Delta h||, which scales linearly with manifold curvature; on curved 1D data, affine models without sufficient correction face an error floor.
AI.conclusion: The nonlinear correction norm acts as an effective-dimension parameter that directly links data-manifold curvature to the sample complexity of compositional learners.

title: Steering Bayesian Inference and Decisions through Data Poisoning
summary: Adversarial machine learning has revealed that statistical models can be manipulated through poisoned data, and Bayesian inference is no exception. Earlier work has shown that subtle poisoning attacks can drive the posterior toward a distribution of the attacker's choosing. Such posterior attraction attacks require a fully specified target posterior; however, attackers typically care about only a few posterior quantities or, more consequentially, about a downstream decision. Herein, we study how an attacker can alter Bayesian inference and decisions by deleting or replicating a few observations, chosen to minimize the maximum mean discrepancy between the resulting posterior and a target distribution. A suitable kernel lets the attacker steer selected posterior moments without specifying the rest of the target. Because Bayes actions depend on the posterior only through expected utilities, which are themselves posterior moments, the same approach can target a decision directly. We construct the attacks with a gradient-based heuristic that requires only posterior samples, and analyze its convergence. Experiments with regression and hierarchical models compare moment-based and full-posterior attacks, and illustrate how deleting a handful of observations can flip a Bayesian decision.

AI.tldr: This paper shows how an attacker can steer specific Bayesian posterior moments or downstream decisions by deleting or replicating a few data points via MMD minimization.
AI.motivation: Existing Bayesian data poisoning attacks require specifying a full target posterior, whereas attackers typically aim to manipulate only specific posterior quantities or downstream Bayes decisions.
AI.method: The authors minimize the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) between the poisoned posterior and a target using a kernel tailored to selected posterior moments or expected utilities, solved via a gradient-based heuristic using only posterior samples.
AI.result: Convergence analysis and experiments on regression and hierarchical models compare moment-based and full-posterior attacks, demonstrating that deleting a handful of observations can flip a Bayesian decision.
AI.conclusion: Kernelized MMD poisoning enables targeted manipulation of Bayesian moments and decisions without needing to specify a complete target posterior.

title: A Geometric Understanding of Denoising Autoencoder with Applications to Image Denoising
summary: Denoising autoencoders have shown strong empirical performance in recovering clean data from their noisy observations, yet their underlying statistical behavior remains underexplored. In this paper, we study denoising autoencoders under the manifold hypothesis, assuming that clean data are supported on low-dimensional smooth manifolds embedded in a high-dimensional ambient space, while noisy observations are generated by isotropic Gaussian noise. We establish generalization guarantees in three geometric scenarios: a single manifold, a pairwise separated finite union of manifolds, and a finite union of intersecting manifolds. Using local chart representations, partitions of unity, and neural network approximation, we derive upper bounds for the expected squared reconstruction error for denoising autoencoder. In the single-manifold and separated-union scenarios, the error consists of a sample-dependent statistical term of order $n^{-2/(d+2)}\log^4 n$, a residual term of order $d\sigma^2/D$ caused by tangential noise, and an exponentially small tail term associated with failure of the manifold projection. Here $D$ is the data ambient dimension, $d$ is the intrinsic dimension of the clean-data manifold, and $\sigma^2$ is the expected squared noise magnitude. In the scenario of intersecting manifolds, we further identify an additional ambiguity term determined by the probability mass near the intersection neighborhood. Numerical experiments on synthetic manifolds and real image datasets support the predicted sample-size scaling law and illustrate the additional reconstruction ambiguity near manifold intersections.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes non-asymptotic generalization bounds for denoising autoencoders under the manifold hypothesis across single, separated, and intersecting manifold settings.
AI.motivation: Despite strong empirical success in image denoising, the statistical generalization behavior of denoising autoencoders on low-dimensional manifolds corrupted by high-dimensional isotropic Gaussian noise remains underexplored.
AI.method: Using local chart representations, partitions of unity, and neural network approximation, the authors upper-bound the expected squared reconstruction error for single manifolds, separated unions of manifolds, and intersecting manifolds.
AI.result: For single and separated manifolds, the error decomposes into a statistical term O(n^-2/(d+2) log^4 n), a tangential-noise residual O(d sigma^2 / D), and an exponentially small projection-failure tail, while intersecting manifolds incur an extra ambiguity term near intersections; synthetic and real-image experiments confirm the scaling laws.
AI.conclusion: Manifold geometry and intersection neighborhoods govern the statistical convergence rate and irreducible error floor of denoising autoencoders.

title: Minimax Estimation of Discrete Distributions under Hockey-stick Divergence
summary: We initiate the study of estimating a discrete distribution with respect to the hockey-stick divergence from independent samples. We provide non-asymptotic upper and lower bounds on the minimax expected loss in terms of the alphabet size, the number of samples, and the divergence parameter. The upper bounds are achieved by add-constant estimators, while the lower bound is derived via a Bayes risk argument. Both upper bounds and lower bounds reveal a transition between polynomial and exponential regimes as the parameters of the problem vary.

AI.tldr: This paper initiates the study of minimax discrete distribution estimation under hockey-stick divergence, proving matching upper and lower bounds that reveal polynomial-to-exponential regime transitions.
AI.motivation: Estimating discrete distributions from independent samples is fundamental in statistics, but minimax rates under the hockey-stick divergence had not been characterized.
AI.method: The authors derive non-asymptotic minimax upper bounds using add-constant estimators and matching lower bounds via a Bayes risk argument in terms of alphabet size, sample size, and the divergence parameter.
AI.result: Both upper and lower bounds establish the minimax expected loss and reveal a sharp transition between polynomial and exponential sample-complexity regimes as problem parameters vary.
AI.conclusion: Add-constant estimators achieve minimax-optimal rates for discrete distribution estimation under hockey-stick divergence, with complexity governed by a parameter-dependent phase transition.

title: Joint Learning of Factual and Counterfactual Worlds for Causal Prior-data Fitted Networks
summary: Estimating treatment effects is central to science across many disciplines and requires counterfactual reasoning about alternative worlds. In the real world, however, each unit reveals its outcome only under the factual world. Thus, the factual and counterfactual outcomes can never be jointly learned by any model trained on real data. The problem is therefore tractable only in synthetic settings, where both worlds can be generated. Recent progress on prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) has shown that models pre-trained purely on synthetic data can transfer to real-world prediction. This paradigm has since carried over to causal effect estimation. Despite this fully synthetic setup, existing causal PFNs carry the real-world constraint into their training objective, confining learning to a single world's outcome per unit. The dependence between the two worlds is thereby lost, and the density of the treatment effect relies by default on independence, which is implausible in practice. We therefore propose joint learning, a training setup in which a causal PFN learns the joint distribution of the factual and counterfactual outcomes of each unit. From the joint distribution, we obtain both the response and the individual treatment effect densities, and at inference, we apply optimal transport across units to obtain an approximation of the average treatment effect density. Ours is therefore the first causal PFN approach to provide all three densities together while accounting for the cross-world dependence. We apply joint learning and optimal transport to existing causal PFNs and evaluate it across semi-synthetic, synthetic, and real benchmarks spanning diverse causal scenarios. The jointly trained models significantly improve upon their baselines in point estimation and uncertainty quantification in most settings, indicating that joint learning is a preferable training setup for causal PFNs.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes joint learning of factual and counterfactual outcomes for causal prior-data fitted networks (PFNs), enabling coherent individual and average treatment effect density estimation.
AI.motivation: Existing causal PFNs train on only one world's outcome per synthetic unit, mirroring real-world constraints unnecessarily, which loses cross-world dependence and forces treatment effect densities to assume independence.
AI.method: The authors train causal PFNs on synthetic data to learn the joint distribution of factual and counterfactual outcomes per unit, yielding response and individual treatment effect densities, and apply optimal transport across units at inference to approximate the average treatment effect density.
AI.result: Evaluated across synthetic, semi-synthetic, and real causal benchmarks, jointly trained causal PFNs significantly improve point estimation and uncertainty quantification over single-world baselines in most settings.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting synthetic access to both factual and counterfactual worlds during PFN pre-training captures cross-world dependence and improves causal effect estimation.

title: Learning Autoregressive Neural Operators on Solver-Defined Physical Constraint Manifolds
summary: Autoregressive neural operators approximate time-dependent PDE solvers by repeatedly composing a learned transition, although the resulting states need not remain feasible under the discrete constraints of the numerical problem. We study this issue for incompressible flow, where each velocity state must satisfy solver-level incompressibility together with prescribed boundary values. We formulate autoregressive operator learning as a map between solver-defined affine feasible sets and introduce PCM-NO, a projected-residual realization of this feasible-transition principle.
