The neural backbone predicts a candidate state increment, a fixed tangent projection extracts its admissible component, and a metric retraction maps the advanced state to the prescribed feasible set. With exact affine constraint solves, the resulting transition is closed on the feasible set, while an affine identity separates admissible-update parameterization from state-level closure. With approximate solves, tangent-only residuals admit a cumulative upper bound, whereas per-step retraction resets feasibility to the residual achieved by the current solve. Experiments on periodic Navier--Stokes flow and lid-driven cavity flow demonstrate the superiority of PCM-NO in preserving solver-level constraints over long autoregressive rollouts and under parameter, boundary-value, and resolution shifts, while achieving lower rollout errors and better flow-specific diagnostics across both in-distribution and stress settings.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces PCM-NO, an autoregressive neural operator that preserves solver-defined physical constraints such as incompressibility and boundary conditions via tangent projection and metric retraction.
AI.motivation: Autoregressive neural operators for time-dependent PDEs often drift off the discrete feasible set of numerical constraints during long rollouts.
AI.method: PCM-NO formulates transitions between solver-defined affine feasible sets by predicting a candidate state increment, extracting its admissible component with a fixed tangent projection, and applying a metric retraction to enforce feasibility.
AI.result: Theoretical bounds characterize exact vs. approximate constraint solves, and experiments on periodic Navier-Stokes and lid-driven cavity flows show lower rollout errors, better flow diagnostics, and stronger constraint preservation under parameter, boundary, and resolution shifts.
AI.conclusion: Embedding tangent projection and metric retraction into autoregressive neural operators ensures solver-level physical feasibility over long rollouts and distribution shifts.

title: Tight Sequential Confidence Intervals for Online Kernel Regression
summary: We characterize, in the worst case over kernels, the sharp minimax width of online confidence intervals for elements of a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS). This resolves the open problem posed by Vakili et al. (2021) in its original discrete-time form. A learner observes $y_i=f(x_i)+\epsilon_i$ at adaptively chosen points, with $\|f\|_{\mathcal H_k}\le B$ and i.i.d. $R$-sub-Gaussian noise, and reports the interval $|f(x)-\mu_n(x)|\le\rho_n(\delta)\sigma_n(x)$, where $\mu_n$ and $\sigma_n$ are the posterior mean and standard deviation of a surrogate Gaussian process model with regularization parameter $\lambda$. Writing $\rho_n^*(\delta)$ for the minimax confidence width for a fixed kernel, we show that, for the sum of a linear kernel and a periodic Sobolev kernel, all sufficiently large $n$, and all $\delta\in(0,1/4]$, $\rho_n^*(\delta)\asymp B+(R/\lambda)\sqrt{\gamma_n+\log(1/\delta)}$, where $\gamma_n$ is the maximal information gain and grows polynomially in $n$. Building on Lattimore (2023), we construct an adaptive design on a fixed two-dimensional domain for which, under Gaussian noise, the normalized error at a prespecified point is $\Omega(B+(R/\lambda)\sqrt{\gamma_n})$ with constant probability. This rules out the conjectured polylogarithmic width in the worst case over kernels and online designs.

AI.tldr: This paper resolves an open problem by proving the sharp minimax width of sequential confidence intervals for online kernel regression, ruling out polylogarithmic widths in the worst case.
AI.motivation: Whether online RKHS confidence intervals could achieve polylogarithmic width in the worst case over kernels and adaptive designs (posed by Vakili et al., 2021) remained an open question.
AI.method: For a surrogate GP model with regularization lambda and maximal information gain gamma_n, the authors construct an adaptive 2D design under Gaussian noise using the sum of a linear kernel and a periodic Sobolev kernel.
AI.result: They prove the minimax confidence width scales as Theta(B + (R/lambda) sqrt(gamma_n + log(1/delta))), showing a constant-probability normalized error of Omega(B + (R/lambda) sqrt(gamma_n)) at a prespecified point where gamma_n grows polynomially in n.
AI.conclusion: Polynomial dependence on maximal information gain is unavoidable in worst-case online kernel regression confidence intervals, settling the Vakili et al. open problem.

title: Conditional Asset Pricing Transformer
summary: In this paper, we propose a conditional asset pricing transformer (CAP-T) that captures nonlinear interactions among firms through attention to forecast excess returns. In the first stage, a transformer estimates conditional expected returns, and kernel-weighted principal component analysis of its residuals estimates the local factor loading space. Projecting the conditional mean onto this space separates factor risk compensation from conditional mispricing. Then, in the second stage, separate transformers learn these two components, whose predictions are combined to forecast returns. As a result, the proposed framework decomposes returns into conditional mispricing, factor risk compensation, a centered factor component, and an unpredictable innovation. We establish approximation and generalization bounds and characterize how first-stage prediction errors propagate through local factor estimation and component learning, providing statistical guaranties for conditional mispricing, factor loadings, and factor risk premia. Finally, simulations and empirical studies demonstrate the predictive and interpretive benefits of the proposed method.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes the Conditional Asset Pricing Transformer (CAP-T), a two-stage attention framework that decomposes excess stock returns into conditional mispricing and factor risk compensation.
AI.motivation: Capturing nonlinear firm interactions while cleanly separating factor risk premia from conditional mispricing with statistical guarantees remains challenging in empirical asset pricing.
AI.method: Stage one uses a transformer to estimate conditional expected returns and applies kernel-weighted PCA to its residuals to estimate local factor loadings; stage two trains separate transformers on the projected factor risk compensation and orthogonal conditional mispricing components.
AI.result: The authors establish approximation and generalization bounds tracking stage-one error propagation to mispricing, loadings, and risk premia, and show improved predictive and interpretive performance in simulations and empirical studies.
AI.conclusion: Combining attention-based return forecasting with kernel-weighted residual PCA yields an interpretable, statistically grounded decomposition of asset returns.

title: Sharp Gaussian Approximation for Q-Learning
summary: Gaussian approximation provides a foundation for online statistical inference in reinforcement learning. We establish sharp non-asymptotic Gaussian approximation rates in Wasserstein distance for asynchronous Q-learning with Polyak-Ruppert averaging. We prove an upper bound of $\widetilde{O}(n^{-1/4})$, where $n$ is the number of iterations, together with a matching lower bound up to logarithmic factors. Q-learning is more challenging to analyze than linear stochastic approximation due to the nonlinearity of the Bellman operator. Asynchronous updates introduce further challenges due to Markovian noise. Our analysis separates the errors from Bellman nonlinearity, Markovian noise, and the finite-sample covariance discrepancy. In particular, we show that Markovian noise induces an unavoidable bias even when the Bellman operator is linear. The trade-off between this bias and the covariance discrepancy determines the convergence rate. We further extend our analysis to the synchronous setting and establish a sharp rate of $\widetilde{O}(n^{-1/2})$.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes sharp non-asymptotic Gaussian approximation rates in Wasserstein distance for asynchronous and synchronous Q-learning with Polyak-Ruppert averaging.
AI.motivation: Online statistical inference in reinforcement learning requires tight Gaussian approximation rates, which are complicated in Q-learning by Bellman operator nonlinearity and Markovian noise from asynchronous updates.
AI.method: The authors separate errors from Bellman nonlinearity, Markovian noise, and finite-sample covariance discrepancy to derive upper and matching lower bounds in Wasserstein distance for Polyak-Ruppert averaged Q-learning.
AI.result: They prove a sharp rate of O_tilde(n^-1/4) for asynchronous Q-learning (with a matching lower bound up to log factors, driven by an unavoidable Markovian-noise bias even for linear Bellman operators) and extend it to O_tilde(n^-1/2) for synchronous Q-learning.
AI.conclusion: The trade-off between Markovian-noise bias and covariance discrepancy fundamentally governs the O_tilde(n^-1/4) Gaussian approximation rate of asynchronous Q-learning.

title: Integrating Latent Block Models into Variational Autoencoders for Disentangled Representation Learning
summary: We introduce LBM-VAE, a novel framework that integrates Latent Block Models (LBMs) into Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) to jointly cluster observations and latent dimensions. Beyond its clustering capabilities, LBM-VAE provides a block-structured latent representation that naturally supports disentangled representation learning. In contrast to conventional approaches that associate each factor of variation with an individual latent dimension, our framework allows factors of variation to be encoded across groups of latent dimensions. Experimental results demonstrate the promising clustering performance of LBM-VAE, while achieving competitive results in disentangled representation learning. LBM-VAE highlights the potential of combining co-clustering and variational inference to learn structured and interpretable latent representations.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces LBM-VAE, integrating Latent Block Models into Variational Autoencoders to jointly co-cluster observations and latent dimensions for block-structured disentangled representations.
AI.motivation: Conventional disentangled VAEs tie each factor of variation to a single latent dimension, limiting their ability to represent factors distributed across groups of latent dimensions.
AI.method: LBM-VAE embeds a Latent Block Model into the VAE latent space to simultaneously cluster observations and group latent dimensions into coherent blocks.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate promising co-clustering performance alongside competitive disentangled representation learning compared to existing approaches.
AI.conclusion: Combining co-clustering with variational inference enables VAEs to learn structured, interpretable representations where factors of variation span groups of latent dimensions.

title: The Manifold-Index Model: provably and efficiently avoiding the statistical and computational curse of dimensionality
summary: We study vector-valued regression with predictors filling a tube around an unknown $m$-dimensional manifold $\mathcal{M}$ in $\mathbb{R}^D$. In the Manifold-Index Model, the mean response is $F=f\circ\Pi_{\mathcal{M}}$, where $\Pi_{\mathcal{M}}$ is the nearest-point projection onto $\mathcal{M}$ and $f:\mathcal{M}\to\mathbb{R}^p$ is a possibly non-injective link function. Multiscale ANisotropic lOcal Regression (MANOR) estimates tangent planes by multiscale PCA of predictors with similar responses, then refines them by pooling outer products of local slopes. The neighborhoods narrow tangentially while retaining complete normal fibers. We assume a Lipschitz link differential and bounded response noise. For $p\ge m$, under our geometric and sampling conditions, $n$ independent observations give mean tangent-space error of order $n^{-2/(m+4)}$ and integrated squared prediction error at the $m$-dimensional nonparametric rate $n^{-4/(m+4)}$, up to logarithmic factors. In a scaling regime with fixed intrinsic dimension, model and scale parameters, and ratio of manifold volume to the $m$-th power of its reach, the required sample size grows polynomially in $D+p$, and computation is polynomial in $n$, $D$ and $p$. Numerical experiments on curves with non-monotone links and surfaces with vector-valued responses compare observed convergence rates with the theoretical bounds; a Langevin dynamics example tests prediction of hitting probabilities under an approximate manifold-index model.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes the Manifold-Index Model and the MANOR estimator for vector-valued regression on tubular manifold data, achieving intrinsic-dimension rates in polynomial time and sample complexity.
AI.motivation: High-dimensional regression around an unknown m-dimensional manifold suffers from the curse of dimensionality unless both statistical rates and computation scale with intrinsic rather than ambient dimension.
AI.method: Multiscale ANisotropic lOcal Regression (MANOR) estimates tangent planes via multiscale PCA on response-similar neighborhoods that narrow tangentially while retaining full normal fibers, then pools outer products of local slopes.
AI.result: Under a Lipschitz link differential and p >= m, n samples yield O(n^-2/(m+4)) tangent-space error and O(n^-4/(m+4)) integrated squared prediction error (up to log factors), with sample size and compute polynomial in D and p; experiments on curves, surfaces, and Langevin hitting probabilities confirm the rates.
AI.conclusion: Anisotropic multiscale local regression provably and efficiently circumvents the ambient curse of dimensionality in manifold-index regression.

title: Measuring Coherence in Predictive Models
summary: Many sequential decision-making procedures, such as active learning, implicitly assume that a model's current predictions agree with those it expects to make after updating on new data, a property we call coherence. Most models in use do not update by exact conditioning and are not guaranteed to be coherent, which can lead to worse decisions. Yet there is currently no general way to measure incoherence or to tell when it matters. We develop tools to measure incoherence and characterise when it affects decisions. We introduce the incoherence ratio, an MMD-based measure of how far any updating procedure departs from coherence, computed only from the procedure's own predictions and updates, and accompany it with an anytime-valid test of coherence. In Bayesian experimental design, acquisition objectives that are equivalent for coherent models choose different data under every approximate model we study, and the incoherence ratio tracks how far incoherence distorts them. We also introduce action coherence, which captures only the incoherence that changes a decision. What a resulting disagreement costs, however, is determined primarily by predictive accuracy. Sequential decisions depend on how a model updates as well as on what it predicts, so coherence, like accuracy, should be checked rather than assumed.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the incoherence ratio, an anytime-valid coherence test, and action coherence to measure when approximate predictive models disagree with their own future updates.
AI.motivation: Sequential decision procedures like active learning assume models update coherently by exact conditioning, yet approximate models violate coherence without a general way to measure it or assess its decision impact.
AI.method: The authors define the MMD-based incoherence ratio from a model's own predictions and updates, pair it with an anytime-valid test, and define action coherence to isolate incoherence that alters decisions.
AI.result: In Bayesian experimental design, equivalent acquisition objectives select different data under every tested approximate model, with distortion tracked by the incoherence ratio, while the cost of disagreement depends primarily on predictive accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Because sequential decisions depend on how a model updates as well as what it predicts, coherence should be explicitly measured and tested rather than assumed.

title: Generalized Prediction Set with Bandit Feedback
summary: In high-stakes environments where uncertainties abound, set-valued prediction offers a cautious and robust mechanism by presenting multiple potential labels as the prediction for each test instance to mitigate the potential risk associated with prediction errors. Yet, integrating this paradigm with out-of-distribution (OOD) detection remains scarcely explored in such settings as online learning with bandit feedback. The bandit feedback mechanism informs the learner about the correctness of the pulled arm/action instead of the explicit ground truth label, leaving the true class label unknown when an incorrect action is taken. To address this challenge, we introduce BanditGPS which conducts set-valued prediction with OOD detection in the bandit feedback setting, using an estimation to the ground truth of class labels. BanditGPS achieves three objectives: render small/informative prediction sets, enhance the OOD detection performance, and control the recall for all normal classes to meet prescribed requirements. Our approach is characterized by the loss function, which trades off between high OOD detection and small prediction sets. Theoretically, we prove that the convergence rate of the regret is $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{-1/2})$. The empirical results further show that BanditGPS effectively controls the recalls with promising performances on OOD detection and informative prediction.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces BanditGPS, an online set-valued prediction framework with out-of-distribution (OOD) detection under bandit feedback.
AI.motivation: High-stakes online learning with bandit feedback only reveals whether a pulled arm was correct rather than the true class label, making it difficult to combine informative prediction sets, OOD detection, and class-wise recall control.
AI.method: BanditGPS estimates ground-truth class labels from bandit feedback and optimizes a loss function that trades off small prediction sets against high OOD detection while enforcing prescribed recall constraints across normal classes.
AI.result: Theoretically, BanditGPS achieves an O_tilde(T^-1/2) regret convergence rate, and empirical results confirm effective recall control alongside strong OOD detection and informative prediction sets.
AI.conclusion: Estimating class labels from bandit feedback within a constrained trade-off loss enables reliable set-valued prediction and OOD detection in online environments.

title: High-dimensional transfer learning with unaligned ordinal responses
summary: In this work, we study high-dimensional transfer learning with unaligned ordinal responses, allowing different domain-specific regression coefficients, cumulative links and thresholds. We develop the sample-split and full-target algorithms that pool source and target likelihoods and then estimate a target correction. Under suitable conditions, our algorithms achieve minimax-optimal rates for parameter estimation and excess risk. Simulations favor the full-target algorithm over the sample-split algorithm for finite-sample estimation and prediction. An application to a medical dataset further demonstrates the predictive gains of our full-target algorithm over the target-only and pooled baselines when transferring information from the five-category source data to binary hospital mortality.

AI.tldr: This paper develops minimax-optimal transfer learning algorithms for high-dimensional ordinal regression with unaligned responses, differing coefficients, and domain-specific thresholds.
AI.motivation: Transferring knowledge across ordinal response datasets is challenging when source and target domains have unaligned categories, different cumulative links, and distinct regression parameters.
AI.method: The authors propose sample-split and full-target algorithms that pool source and target likelihoods before estimating a target-specific correction.
AI.result: Both algorithms achieve minimax-optimal rates for parameter estimation and excess risk; simulations favor the full-target algorithm in finite samples, and transferring 5-category source data to binary hospital mortality improves prediction over target-only and pooled baselines.
AI.conclusion: Likelihood pooling with target correction enables minimax-optimal high-dimensional transfer learning even when ordinal response scales are unaligned across domains.

title: The Limits of Closed-Form Couplings for Few-Step Generation
summary: Few-step generators via flow models require complicated technical solutions such as a pretrained flow model or a consistency loss. While rectified flows have gained popularity for their success in few-step sampling, they pay a cost of needing a pre-trained model and sampling a large number of couplings per dataset. Yet for a finite dataset and a Gaussian probability path, the probability-flow vector field of the empirical distribution is available in closed form, so one could use this field as the teacher and skip pretraining altogether. We demonstrate that, surprisingly, this approach is impossible for problems of practical relevance. In particular, the analytic solution of the diffusion process in high dimensions becomes almost a linear transformation. The integration returns the noise vector drawn at initialisation, plus a drift that is empirically a faint copy of the data point, almost independent of the noise. The coupling therefore differs from an independent pairing only through this drift. As a result, training a model on these couplings is almost equivalent to training the model on the independent draws of the noise and the data, which does not provide a useful teacher. We highlight that this is the direct consequence of the high-dimensionality of the data, and that for low enough dimensions or large enough datasets, analytic couplings become more efficient teachers. We quantify this effect by the fraction of endpoint energy carried by the drift, which scales as $\frac{\log N}{d}$ for a dataset of size $N$ in a $d$-dimensional space. Finally, we provide an empirical study confirming all the theoretical results presented in the paper.

AI.tldr: This paper proves that using the closed-form empirical probability-flow vector field as a teacher for few-step flow models fails in high dimensions because the resulting couplings degenerate to near-independent pairings.
AI.motivation: Because the probability-flow ODE of an empirical dataset under a Gaussian path has a closed-form vector field, it could in principle replace expensive pretrained teachers in rectified-flow distillation.
AI.method: The authors analyze the high-dimensional analytic diffusion solution and quantify the drift energy fraction carried by the empirical coupling as a function of dataset size N and dimension d.
AI.result: In high dimensions, the integration returns initial noise plus a faint data drift whose energy fraction scales as (log N)/d, making training on empirical couplings nearly equivalent to training on independent noise-data pairs, as confirmed empirically.
AI.conclusion: Closed-form empirical couplings cannot serve as useful few-step teachers unless d is small or N is exponentially large, explaining why pretrained teachers or consistency losses remain necessary.

title: Compressed Simulation-Based Inference: Neural Posterior Estimation for Massive Data via Low-Dimensional Sketches
summary: Neural posterior estimation (NPE) is a popular Bayesian simulation-based inference (SBI) approach that uses neural networks trained on simulated data--parameter pairs to approximate the posterior given a user-chosen prior. For high-dimensional observations, NPE methods typically approximate the conditional density of the parameter given a user-chosen or learned summary statistic, rather than the entire dataset, due to the curse of dimensionality. However, both approaches face challenges: hand-crafting good summaries for complex models requires considerable effort from scientists, while learning them from massive datasets can be prohibitively computationally expensive. To address these challenges, we propose approximating the conditional density of a parameter given low-dimensional sketches of the data. We show that, for a model with a $p$-dimensional parameter, only $2p+1$ random sketches are needed for posterior consistency. We compare with state-of-the-art embedding networks for NPE, and we find that our method \emph{matches} the best embedding network's performance while \emph{increasing computational efficiency}.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes compressed neural posterior estimation (NPE) using 2p + 1 random low-dimensional data sketches, matching state-of-the-art embedding networks with higher computational efficiency.
AI.motivation: For massive high-dimensional datasets in simulation-based inference, hand-crafting summary statistics is labor-intensive while learning neural embedding networks is computationally expensive.
AI.method: The authors approximate the parameter posterior conditioned on random low-dimensional sketches of the data rather than learned or hand-crafted summaries.
AI.result: They prove that 2p + 1 random sketches suffice for posterior consistency in a p-dimensional parameter model, and experiments show the method matches top NPE embedding networks while improving computational efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Low-dimensional random sketches provide a theoretically grounded, computationally cheap alternative to learned summary networks in neural posterior estimation.

title: Comments on "Deep Fréchet Regression"
comment: Comment on arXiv:2407.21407 ("Deep Fréchet Regression"). This discussion comment will appear in the Journal of the American Statistical Association (JASA)
summary: We discuss the Journal of the American Statistical Association (JASA) discussion paper "Deep Fréchet Regression" and explore an alternative perspective based on conditional flow matching. We propose learning covariate-dependent transport directly within the response space, avoiding separate manifold learning and reverse mapping. This perspective offers a potentially more flexible framework for incorporating geometric structure and modeling full conditional distributions.

AI.tldr: This commentary on "Deep Frechet Regression" proposes an alternative conditional flow matching perspective that learns covariate-dependent transport directly in the response space.
AI.motivation: Separate manifold learning and reverse mapping steps in Deep Frechet Regression may limit flexibility when modeling geometric structure and full conditional distributions.
AI.method: The authors outline learning covariate-dependent transport directly within the response space via conditional flow matching.
AI.result: As a commentary paper, it presents no new experiments and instead frames conditional flow matching as an alternative to separate manifold learning and reverse mapping.
AI.conclusion: Direct response-space conditional flow matching offers a flexible geometric alternative for modeling full conditional distributions in Frechet regression settings.

title: Generative Data Augmentation Without External Data: An Empirical and Theoretical Study on Deep Networks
summary: Generative data augmentation adds samples from generative models to a classifier's training set. Many influential studies use generators pre-trained on large external datasets, and so mix the value of synthetic data with knowledge transferred through pretraining. We study the case without external data, where each generator learns only from the classifier's own training set, and ask when and why adding generated samples to that training set raises or lowers the classifier's test accuracy. We train classifiers with four backbones on six datasets, two of them medical, adding samples from four generators. We bound the excess risk of a classifier trained with synthetic data, that is, how far its population risk can lie above the minimum risk within its hypothesis class. The bound charges synthetic data for the total variation distance between the real and generated distributions and credits synthetic data for a larger training set. The gain from adding synthetic data, the fall in population risk, is at most the excess risk of the real-only classifier, which trains on the real images alone. Read through the bound, the experiments suggest that synthetic data help most when our classifiers detect only a small discrepancy between the generated and real data and the real-only classifier has room to improve, and that synthetic data help little or hurt when the detected discrepancy is large. Generators with a larger lower bound on the total variation distance, a bound that we estimate from our own classifiers, tend to help less on five of the six datasets, and on the CIFAR datasets the most accurate backbone gains the least. The bound gives these directions but not the size of the largest gains, most of which traditional augmentation also reaches at the same number of optimizer steps.

AI.tldr: This empirical and theoretical study characterizes when generative data augmentation without external data helps or hurts classifier accuracy, showing gains depend on total variation distance and real-only excess risk.
AI.motivation: Prior studies of generative data augmentation often use externally pre-trained generators, conflating the value of synthetic samples with external pretraining knowledge.
AI.method: The authors train four classifier backbones on six datasets (including two medical datasets) augmented by four generators trained solely on each classifier's own training set, and derive an excess-risk bound charging synthetic data for total variation (TV) distance to real data.
AI.result: Synthetic data help most when classifier-estimated TV lower bounds are small and real-only excess risk has room to improve, and help little or hurt when discrepancy is large; on five of six datasets larger TV bounds yield smaller gains, and traditional augmentation matches most of the largest gains at equal optimizer steps.
AI.conclusion: Without external pretraining, generative augmentation is bounded by real-only excess risk and generator-real TV discrepancy, rarely surpassing well-tuned traditional augmentation.

title: Endogenous Preferences as Vulnerability Signals: Discovering Universal Adversarial Triggers for LLM Utility Degradation
summary: Deployed large language models must remain useful when untrusted text enters their prompt context. Adversarial prompting and red-teaming methods typically define the failures they seek through task labels, harmful targets, judge feedback, or downstream utility scores. We ask whether a frozen model's clean behavior can reveal a reusable context vulnerability when its task-level form is unknown, and downstream task feedback is withheld. To study this question, EndoUT uses a Siamese-style design that compares the same frozen victim on clean and span-modified versions of each unlabeled instruction. Without a task-level target, the clean pass supplies the victim's preferred response-onset token as an instruction-conditioned reference; Endogenous Preference Disruption (EPD) measures how insertion weakens that preference. An auxiliary generator supplies bounded-span proposals; EPD guides its update and ranks the pool without access to downstream information. The highest-scoring victim-specific span is fixed before evaluation and reused unchanged across all held-out inputs. Across four instruction-tuned models and nine benchmarks, fixed triggers reduce benign-task utility by 40.2 percentage points on average, with negative mean change on every benchmark and greater average degradation than every evaluated baseline under the reported protocols. Matched protocol ablations show stronger transfer for source-side selection followed by fixed reuse than for null-context fixed reuse or per-input generation. Transfer recurs across proposers with proposal-dependent strength; output-level analyses identify victim-specific associations between trigger families and downstream failure patterns. Thus, clean behavior can expose context vulnerabilities that transfer across inputs yet manifest through structured, victim-specific patterns of utility degradation. The code and data will be released upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces EndoUT, a method that discovers universal adversarial triggers for LLM utility degradation using only a frozen model's clean behavior without task labels or downstream feedback. Fixed triggers selected by EndoUT reduce benign-task utility by 40.2 percentage points on average across four instruction-tuned models and nine benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing adversarial prompting and red-teaming methods rely on task labels, harmful targets, judge feedback, or downstream utility scores. They cannot detect reusable context vulnerabilities when the task-level failure form is unknown and downstream feedback is withheld.
AI.method: EndoUT uses a Siamese-style design comparing a frozen victim model on clean and span-modified versions of unlabeled instructions. The clean pass provides the preferred response-onset token as a reference, and Endogenous Preference Disruption (EPD) measures how an inserted span weakens that preference to guide an auxiliary generator and rank candidate triggers.
AI.result: Across four instruction-tuned models and nine benchmarks, fixed triggers reduce benign-task utility by 40.2 percentage points on average, with negative mean change on every benchmark and greater degradation than all evaluated baselines. Ablations show stronger transfer for source-side selection with fixed reuse than for null-context reuse or per-input generation.
AI.conclusion: Clean model behavior can expose context vulnerabilities that transfer across inputs and manifest as structured, victim-specific patterns of utility degradation.

title: Theoretical Foundations of Computational Islamic Jurisprudence (Fiqh)
summary: This paper presents the theoretical foundations and a comprehensive formal system for Computational Islamic Jurisprudence (Fiqh). We begin by establishing six foundational principles that distinguish computational Fiqh from conventional natural language processing and general theological formalization. These principles define Islamic jurisprudence as a normative deductive science operating on empirically grounded facts, necessitating a dual inductive-deductive methodology, and requiring a logical foundation specifically engineered for Fiqh rather than adopted from existing formalisms. Based on these principles, we construct a three-layer stratified computational language, $\mathcal{F} = D \circ A \circ G$, consisting of: (1) an Arabic Morphological/Grammatical Grounding Engine that transforms fully vocalized Classical Arabic into language-independent Grounded Action Structures (GAS); (2) the Arabic Reified Action Calculus (ARAC) that normalizes these structures into canonical logical representations; and (3) a function-free Horn-clause Datalog engine for executable legal deduction. Furthermore, we introduce a bridging methodology (Algorithm $\Omega$) that dynamically generates a Fiqh-Categorized Attribute Grammar from inductively extracted Horn clauses via an Ontological Meta-Map ($\mathcal{M}_{onto}$), seamlessly connecting the inductive extraction of legal rules to their deductive application. The paper rigorously proves the system's semantic correctness, representational completeness, termination, and decidability. Crucially, by leveraging morphosyntactic inflection markers ($\delta$ modes) as structural constraints, we prove the strict unambiguity of the proposed grammar, achieving deterministic $O(n)$ linear parsing complexity. This work provides a mathematically verifiable, epistemologically grounded, and computationally tractable foundation for automated Islamic jurisprudence.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes theoretical foundations and a formal three-layer computational system for Computational Islamic Jurisprudence (Fiqh). It proves semantic correctness, representational completeness, termination, decidability, and deterministic O(n) linear parsing complexity.
AI.motivation: Computational Fiqh differs from conventional NLP and general theological formalization because it operates as a normative deductive science on empirically grounded facts, requiring a dual inductive-deductive methodology and a purpose-built logical foundation.
AI.method: The authors define six foundational principles and construct a three-layer stratified language F = D o A o G: an Arabic Morphological/Grammatical Grounding Engine producing Grounded Action Structures (GAS), the Arabic Reified Action Calculus (ARAC) for canonical logical normalization, and a function-free Horn-clause Datalog engine for legal deduction. Algorithm Omega dynamically generates a Fiqh-Categorized Attribute Grammar from inductively extracted Horn clauses via an Ontological Meta-Map.
AI.result: The paper rigorously proves the system's semantic correctness, representational completeness, termination, and decidability. Using morphosyntactic inflection markers (delta modes) as structural constraints, it proves strict grammar unambiguity and deterministic O(n) linear parsing complexity.
AI.conclusion: This work provides a mathematically verifiable, epistemologically grounded, and computationally tractable foundation for automated Islamic jurisprudence.

title: Whose Side Are You On? Measuring Stance at Scale for Reddit Discourse Analysis During the Israel-Gaza War
comment: Code is available at: this https URL
summary: Large-scale discourse analysis often requires stance labels, yet for many high-salience political events such labels are unavailable at the comment level. We introduce and validate a comment-level stance measurement instrument that assigns Pro-Israel, Pro-Palestinian, or Undefined stance using Reddit comment text. The instrument is calibrated from a small, manually annotated gold-standard dataset and scaled through large language model-assisted labeling, achieving weighted-$F_{1}=0.88$ against held-out human annotations. To enable corpus-scale measurement, we operationalize the instrument as a lightweight classifier based on DistilBERT embeddings and an RBF SVM, which achieves weighted-$F_{1}=0.7935$ on the original gold-standard set. Applying this instrument, we measure the stance of approximately 2.7 million Reddit comments posted between 2023 and 2025 during the Israel-Gaza war. We demonstrate what this measurement enables by analyzing stance-conditioned asymmetries in sentiment, toxicity, and emotional framing across political affiliations. This work shows how validated, low-cost stance measurement can support large-scale descriptive analysis of polarized discourse, without relying on network structure or prior labeled corpora.

AI.tldr: This paper develops and validates a comment-level stance measurement instrument for Reddit discourse during the Israel-Gaza war, scaling it to analyze 2.7 million comments. It reveals stance-conditioned asymmetries in sentiment, toxicity, and emotional framing across political affiliations.
AI.motivation: Large-scale discourse analysis requires comment-level stance labels, which are often unavailable for high-salience political events without relying on network structure or prior labeled corpora.
AI.method: The authors calibrate a stance instrument (Pro-Israel, Pro-Palestinian, or Undefined) from a small manually annotated gold-standard dataset, scale it via LLM-assisted labeling, and operationalize it as a lightweight classifier using DistilBERT embeddings and an RBF SVM.
AI.result: The LLM-assisted labeling achieves weighted-F1 = 0.88 against held-out human annotations, and the DistilBERT + RBF SVM classifier achieves weighted-F1 = 0.7935 on the gold-standard set. Applied to 2.7 million Reddit comments from 2023 to 2025, the instrument uncovers stance-conditioned asymmetries in sentiment, toxicity, and emotional framing.
AI.conclusion: Validated, low-cost stance measurement can effectively support large-scale descriptive analysis of polarized online discourse without network structure or large prior labeled corpora.

title: Profiling Hallucinations in Frontier LLMs for Entity Linking to Medical Ontologies
comment: The 8th Workshop on Clinical Natural Language Processing at LREC 2026
summary: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into healthcare promises to revolutionize clinical documentation and interoperability, yet reliability remains a concern. This study presents a comprehensive analysis of hallucinations by frontier LLMs tasked with mapping clinical text to SNOMED CT. Through rigorous experimentation, we identify a critical reliability gap: LLMs hallucinate medical codes at a rate that currently renders them unsuitable for autonomous clinical coding applications. Paradoxically, constraining models to use ground-truth mention spans exacerbates, rather than mitigates, these hallucinations. We further contribute a taxonomy of hallucination types--including deprecated codes and cross-ontology errors--and demonstrate that general-purpose LLMs significantly underperform compared to specialized zero-shot entity linking approaches. These findings underscore the need for robust verification mechanisms before clinical deployment.

AI.tldr: This study profiles hallucinations in frontier LLMs when linking clinical text to SNOMED CT, finding that LLMs hallucinate medical codes at rates unsuitable for autonomous clinical coding. Constraining models to ground-truth mention spans unexpectedly worsens hallucinations.
AI.motivation: Integrating LLMs into healthcare for clinical documentation and interoperability requires reliable mapping to medical ontologies like SNOMED CT, yet the extent and nature of LLM code hallucinations remain insufficiently understood.
AI.method: The authors evaluate frontier LLMs on mapping clinical text to SNOMED CT, test the effect of constraining models to ground-truth mention spans, construct a taxonomy of hallucination types (including deprecated codes and cross-ontology errors), and compare against specialized zero-shot entity linking approaches.
AI.result: Frontier LLMs hallucinate medical codes at high rates and significantly underperform specialized zero-shot entity linking methods. Paradoxically, constraining LLMs to ground-truth mention spans exacerbates rather than mitigates hallucinations.
AI.conclusion: Current general-purpose LLMs are unsuitable for autonomous clinical coding and require robust verification mechanisms before clinical deployment.

title: Between the Lines: Multi-turn Contextual Investment Advice Detection
summary: As large language models (LLMs) increasingly power financial conversational assistants, detecting investment advice in natural language has become a critical regulatory and safety challenge. Unlike explicit single-turn recommendations, investment advice often emerges implicitly and progressively over multi-turn conversations, shaped by user intent, delivery style, and contextual buildup. We introduce the first comprehensive framework for detecting both sequential and contextual investment advice in dialogue settings. Central to our approach is a modular, top-down synthetic data generation pipeline that systematically spans a taxonomy of advisory trajectories using an axis-bucket-descriptor schema. We simulate both benign and high-risk conversations across diverse user personas, financial instruments, and risk tiers, and evaluate detection capabilities using LLM-as-a-Judge with entropy-based uncertainty diagnostics. Our results show that contextual advisory detection remains substantially more challenging than sequential cases, even under few-shot prompting with tailored demonstrations. This work lays the foundation for scalable guardrail development in high-stakes, compliance-sensitive domains, where advisory risk is often subtle, distributed, and perception-dependent.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a framework and synthetic data generation pipeline for detecting sequential and contextual investment advice in multi-turn LLM dialogues. Experiments show that contextual advisory detection is substantially harder than sequential detection, even with few-shot prompting.
AI.motivation: As LLMs power financial conversational assistants, detecting investment advice is a critical regulatory challenge because advice often emerges implicitly and progressively over multi-turn conversations rather than in explicit single-turn statements.
AI.method: The authors build a modular, top-down synthetic data generation pipeline using an axis-bucket-descriptor schema to simulate benign and high-risk conversations across diverse user personas, financial instruments, and risk tiers, and evaluate detection using LLM-as-a-Judge with entropy-based uncertainty diagnostics.
AI.result: Evaluations demonstrate that contextual advisory detection remains substantially more challenging than sequential cases, even under few-shot prompting with tailored demonstrations.
AI.conclusion: This framework provides a foundation for developing scalable guardrails in high-stakes, compliance-sensitive financial domains where advisory risk is subtle and distributed.

title: ScopeBench: Evaluating Cultural Norm Scope Awareness in LLMs
summary: Safety evaluation in large language models treats harm as culturally invariant, yet a model cannot correctly apply a safety norm without knowing whose norms bind. We introduce ScopeBench, a benchmark that treats cultural scope as a first-class safety dimension. It comprises 3,323 norms spanning 49 countries across nine cultural clusters, each annotated as Universal or Specific. We define three scope error types identically across four evaluation tasks: Scope Inflation, Scope Deflation, and Scope Displacement. Evaluating 21 frontier LLMs across seven model families, we surface three structural failures. First, the dominant error type inverts with prompt format: Scope Deflation reaches 70% in single-answer classification, while Scope Inflation reaches 33% when each candidate culture is judged independently. Second, scope-classification accuracy is empirically decoupled from behavioral safety: the six classifiers achieving at least 97% Task 1 accuracy still produce harmful responses to 40-42% of scope-violating statements. Third, no model is safe in interaction, with harmful-response rates ranging from 29% to 51% across the cohort, excluding one model that systematically refuses the task. We release all data, code, and model outputs to establish cultural scope as a distinct alignment axis.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces ScopeBench, a benchmark of 3,323 cultural norms across 49 countries to evaluate cultural norm scope awareness in LLMs. Evaluating 21 frontier LLMs reveals that scope-classification accuracy is decoupled from behavioral safety and that no model is safe in interaction.
AI.motivation: Current LLM safety evaluations treat harm as culturally invariant, overlooking that a model cannot properly apply a safety norm without knowing whose norms bind.
AI.method: The authors construct ScopeBench with 3,323 norms (annotated as Universal or Specific) spanning 49 countries and nine cultural clusters, and define three scope error types (Scope Inflation, Scope Deflation, and Scope Displacement) across four evaluation tasks.
AI.result: Across 21 frontier LLMs, dominant error types invert with prompt format (Scope Deflation reaches 70% in single-answer classification; Scope Inflation reaches 33% in independent judgment). Six classifiers with at least 97% Task 1 accuracy still produce harmful responses to 40-42% of scope-violating statements, and interactive harmful-response rates range from 29% to 51% across models (excluding one model that systematically refuses).
AI.conclusion: Cultural scope is a distinct alignment axis where high classification accuracy does not guarantee safe model behavior, motivating the release of ScopeBench's data, code, and outputs.

title: Jailbreak LLMs with Linguistic Style as a Hidden Attack Surface
summary: We show that linguistic style is a systematic and previously overlooked attack surface for LLM safety. Across a diverse taxonomy of styles and multiple state-of-the-art models, stylistic rewrites of identical harmful goals produce order-of-magnitude differences in Attack Success Rate (ASR), with some styles achieving up to 80\% ASR while others remain below 6\%. To exploit this vulnerability, we introduce a lightweight single-pass attack framework that combines a style-conditioned generator with a BERT-based style selector, achieving performance competitive with substantially more expensive multi-turn optimization methods. To understand why style affects safety behavior, we conduct mechanistic analysis on LLaMA-3.1-8B and find that stylistic rewrites disrupt refusal representations while preserving recoverable harmful intent, suggesting a distributed failure mode rather than a single refusal mechanism. Motivated by this finding, we develop a style-aware Direct Preference Optimization defense that reduces ASR from 86\% to 19.5\% while largely preserving utility. Together, our results establish linguistic style as a critical factor in adversarial robustness and provide both mechanistic insight and a practical defense.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that linguistic style is a hidden attack surface for LLM safety, with stylistic rewrites of harmful goals causing order-of-magnitude differences in Attack Success Rate (ASR). It also proposes a lightweight single-pass attack and a style-aware DPO defense.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM safety evaluations overlook how linguistic style systematically affects jailbreak vulnerability and refusal behavior.
AI.method: The authors evaluate stylistic rewrites across a diverse taxonomy of styles, introduce a single-pass attack combining a style-conditioned generator with a BERT-based style selector, conduct mechanistic analysis on LLaMA-3.1-8B, and develop a style-aware Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) defense.
AI.result: Stylistic rewrites yield ASRs ranging from below 6% to 80%, and the single-pass attack matches more expensive multi-turn optimization methods. Mechanistic analysis shows style disrupts refusal representations while preserving harmful intent, and style-aware DPO reduces ASR from 86% to 19.5% while largely preserving utility.
AI.conclusion: Linguistic style is a critical factor in adversarial robustness, and style-aware preference optimization provides an effective defense against distributed refusal failures.

title: Internal Verdicts Track Evidence: A Template-Controlled Neutrosophic Reading of Epistemic States in Large Language Models via the Jacobian Lens
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Published in Neutrosophic Sets and Systems, Vol. 101 (2026). Code, stimuli and data: this https URL
summary: For twenty-five years, neutrosophic logic has assigned independent degrees of truth (T), indeterminacy (I), and falsity (F) to epistemic states that classical and fuzzy semantics cannot express. Previous applications measured these components on outputs: answers, judgments, expert evaluations. This paper reports, to our knowledge, the first neutrosophic reading of components inside the internal representations of a large language model. Using the recently released Jacobian lens on Qwen3.5-4B, we project intermediate-layer readouts onto lexicons of support, refutation, and hedging, obtaining layer-wise (T, I, F) profiles under conflicting evidence, first-person false belief, and factual control (n = 20 each). A first battery yielded three striking signatures: a surge of refutation mass under conflict, sustained indeterminacy under false belief, and an apparent "verdict collapse" before the output layer. A second, template-controlled battery showed that all three, as initially stated, were largely artifacts of prompt grammar: matched templates with agreeing evidence inflate the same lexicon masses, true beliefs elicit the same hedging, and the model verbalizes its verdict when allowed to generate. What survives the controls is stronger than what died: the neutrosophic verdict balance B = log10(F) - log10(T) tracks evidence polarity under identical templates (about 3 orders of magnitude of separation, Cohen's d = 2.3-2.5, p < 10^-6 in 9 of 9 layers; paired Wilcoxon: median difference +2.4 orders, 19/20 items, p = 3.8x10^-6) and residually discriminates false from true first-person beliefs. We argue that the independence of the neutrosophic components is what keeps the common-mode channel observable, making both the measurement and its self-correction possible, and we distill the two-battery design into a reusable protocol for auditing language model internals with lens-based readouts.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first neutrosophic reading of internal LLM representations using the Jacobian lens on Qwen3.5-4B to measure truth (T), indeterminacy (I), and falsity (F) under conflicting evidence and false beliefs. Template-controlled experiments show that the neutrosophic verdict balance tracks evidence polarity across all layers.
AI.motivation: Previous neutrosophic logic applications only measured T, I, and F on model outputs, leaving internal epistemic states in LLM representations unexplored.
AI.method: Using the Jacobian lens on Qwen3.5-4B, the authors project intermediate-layer readouts onto support, refutation, and hedging lexicons across conflicting evidence, first-person false belief, and factual control prompts (n = 20 each), followed by a template-controlled battery to isolate prompt grammar artifacts.
AI.result: Initial signatures of refutation surges, sustained indeterminacy, and verdict collapse were largely prompt-grammar artifacts. Under template controls, the neutrosophic verdict balance B = log10(F) - log10(T) tracks evidence polarity with about 3 orders of magnitude separation (Cohen's d = 2.3-2.5, p < 10^-6 in 9 of 9 layers; paired Wilcoxon median difference +2.4 orders, p = 3.8x10^-6) and residually discriminates false from true first-person beliefs.
AI.conclusion: Independent neutrosophic components keep the common-mode channel observable, enabling a reusable two-battery protocol for auditing LLM internals with lens-based readouts.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Clinical Decision Support in Gait Analysis: A Proof-of-Concept
comment: 12 pages, 2 figures, International Conference on Computational Intelligence
summary: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate significant potential for clinical decision support but lack specialized biomechanical knowledge required for accurate gait analysis interpretation. We developed and evaluated a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework to enhance LLM-generated clinical explanations for ankle fracture rehabilitation using ground reaction force data. Using the GaitRec dataset (503 subjects: 211 healthy, 292 ankle fracture patients), we implemented a five-stage pipeline integrating: (1) machine learning classification (91.3\% accuracy); (2) Layer-wise Relevance Propagation for explainable feature identification; (3) RAG knowledge base from peer-reviewed biomechanics literature; (4) GPT-5 explanation generation with and without retrieval augmentation; and (5) double-blind evaluation by experienced physical therapists across five clinical criteria. RAG augmentation produced statistically significant improvements in Clini-cal Benefit (mean difference=0.60, p=0.047, {\delta}=0.49) and Completeness (mean difference=0.70, p=0.049, {\delta}=0.49), both demonstrating large effect sizes. Baseline GPT-5 achieved strong performance across all criteria (\textgreater4.0/5.0). This proof-of-concept demonstrates that augmenting general-purpose LLMs with domain-specific knowledge meaningfully enhances actionable, evidence-based clinical guidance---dimensions most critical for rehabilitation decision-making. The framework provides a scalable approach for integrating AI into specialized clinical workflows without costly model retraining.

AI.tldr: This proof-of-concept develops and evaluates a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework to enhance GPT-5 clinical explanations for ankle fracture rehabilitation using gait analysis data. RAG significantly improves Clinical Benefit and Completeness in double-blind evaluations by physical therapists.
AI.motivation: General-purpose LLMs show promise for clinical decision support but lack the specialized biomechanical knowledge needed to accurately interpret gait analysis data.
AI.method: Using the GaitRec dataset (503 subjects: 211 healthy, 292 ankle fracture patients), the authors build a five-stage pipeline combining ML classification, Layer-wise Relevance Propagation, a peer-reviewed biomechanics RAG knowledge base, GPT-5 explanation generation with and without RAG, and double-blind evaluation by physical therapists.
AI.result: The ML classifier achieves 91.3% accuracy, and baseline GPT-5 scores above 4.0/5.0 across all criteria. Adding RAG produces statistically significant improvements in Clinical Benefit (mean difference = 0.60, p = 0.047, delta = 0.49) and Completeness (mean difference = 0.70, p = 0.049, delta = 0.49).
AI.conclusion: Augmenting general-purpose LLMs with domain-specific biomechanical literature meaningfully enhances actionable, evidence-based clinical guidance without costly model retraining.

title: One Question, Four Voices: How Advice for Alzheimer's Caregiving Differs Between Caregivers, Clinicians, and Large Language Models
comment: Accepted to ACM CSCW 2026. 35 pages, 7 figures
summary: Online caregiver forums are an important source of emotional and informational support for Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD). We compare responses to 85 real caregiver questions from ALZConnected across four responder groups: peer caregivers, physicians, ChatGPT, and a retrieval-augmented CareGPT grounded in peer discussions. Using 28 measures spanning linguistic form, emotional support, informational support, and topic scope, we examine how these voices differ when answering the same questions. Peers provided time-anchored narratives and community grounding; clinicians offered concise, advice-forward, clinically bounded guidance; and LLMs produced a formal, verbose, highly structured consultation style. CareGPT showed minimal measurable separation from ChatGPT, suggesting that retrieval plus prompt injection alone was insufficient to shift communicative stance. LLM outputs scored higher than peers on politeness and emotion-support markers and were comparable to clinicians on informativeness and physician-alignment measures, but were less narrative and less contextually situated. Topic modeling showed that LLM responses concentrated on advice-oriented themes, whereas peers covered a broader range, including emotional processing, legal and financial concerns, and daily care. These findings suggest that AI can complement, but not replace, human contributions to ADRD caregiver support and motivate hybrid systems that combine structured AI delivery with the distinct strengths of human voices.

AI.tldr: This study compares responses to 85 real Alzheimer's caregiver questions across peer caregivers, clinicians, ChatGPT, and a retrieval-augmented CareGPT using 28 linguistic and content measures. While LLMs match clinicians on informativeness, they differ markedly from human voices in narrative grounding and topic breadth.
AI.motivation: Online caregiver forums provide vital emotional and informational support for Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD), but how LLM advice compares to peer caregivers and clinicians across communicative dimensions is unclear.
AI.method: The authors analyze responses to 85 questions from ALZConnected across four groups (peers, physicians, ChatGPT, and CareGPT grounded in peer discussions) using 28 measures spanning linguistic form, emotional support, informational support, and topic modeling.
AI.result: Peers provide time-anchored narratives and broad topic coverage (including emotional processing, legal, and financial concerns), while clinicians give concise, bounded guidance. LLMs produce formal, verbose, advice-focused responses scoring higher than peers on politeness and emotion-support markers and matching clinicians on informativeness, with CareGPT showing minimal separation from ChatGPT.
AI.conclusion: AI can complement but not replace human voices in ADRD caregiver support, motivating hybrid systems that combine structured AI delivery with human narrative and community grounding.

title: Enhanced English-Sanskrit Translation using Multilingual NMT Approach
summary: Neural Machine Translation (NMT) is a widely accepted technique of automatic translation tasks of Natural Language Processing. However, NMT requires a sufficient amount of parallel corpora to attain a reasonable translation quality. In this work, we have considered a low-resource English-Sanskrit pair for English-to-Sanskrit and Sanskrit-to-English translation. We have performed a comparative analysis by exploring bilingual and multilingual approaches using LSTM-based Sequence-to-Sequence, and fine-tuning a pretrained model IndicTrans in a multilingual NMT approach. To investigate multilingual transfer learning, we additionally construct multilingual translation settings by incorporating Hindi along with English and Sanskrit using language-tagged data. Experimental results demonstrate that IndicTrans-based multilingual models outperform baseline results in terms of automatic evaluation metrics such as BLEU and ChrF for both directions of translation.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates low-resource English-Sanskrit and Sanskrit-English neural machine translation by comparing bilingual and multilingual approaches, including adding Hindi. Fine-tuned multilingual IndicTrans models outperform LSTM-based baselines in both translation directions.
AI.motivation: Neural Machine Translation requires large parallel corpora to achieve good quality, which is lacking for the low-resource English-Sanskrit language pair.
AI.method: The authors compare bilingual and multilingual NMT setups using LSTM-based Sequence-to-Sequence models and fine-tuned pretrained IndicTrans models, incorporating Hindi alongside English and Sanskrit via language-tagged data for multilingual transfer learning.
AI.result: Experimental results show that IndicTrans-based multilingual models outperform baseline models on automatic evaluation metrics including BLEU and ChrF for both English-to-Sanskrit and Sanskrit-to-English translation.
AI.conclusion: Multilingual transfer learning with pretrained models like IndicTrans effectively improves translation quality for low-resource pairs such as English-Sanskrit.

title: Syntactic Complexity Convergence in Dialogue: Analysis of the Phenomenon and Application to LLM Detection
summary: We revisit the under-explored phenomenon of syntactic complexity convergence in dialogue. Extending prior topic-level analyses to full conversations, we examine five human-human datasets and a set of human-LLM dialogues. We integrate and evaluate a multidimensional set of syntactic complexity metrics to quantify structural variation in dialogue. Our analyses reveal robust syntactic complexity convergence across human-human datasets, especially in task-oriented interactions, and statistical tests confirm that these effects are not due to chance. In contrast, human-LLM dialogues show no significant convergence under individual metrics; however, linear-CKA uncovers a distinct cross-metric convergence pattern. Motivated by these differences, we use syntactic complexity as a feature for detecting LLM-involved dialogue, achieving 96\% accuracy. Our classification results demonstrate its potential without relying on likelihood-based signals such as surprisal, which require a language model as the estimator.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes syntactic complexity convergence in human-human and human-LLM dialogues, finding robust convergence in human-human conversations but a distinct cross-metric pattern in human-LLM dialogues. Using syntactic complexity as a feature achieves 96% accuracy in detecting LLM-involved dialogue.
AI.motivation: Syntactic complexity convergence in full conversations is under-explored, and detecting LLM-involved dialogue currently relies on likelihood-based signals such as surprisal that require a language model estimator.
AI.method: The authors evaluate a multidimensional set of syntactic complexity metrics across five human-human datasets and a set of human-LLM dialogues, apply linear-CKA to inspect cross-metric convergence, and train a classifier using syntactic complexity features to detect LLM-involved dialogue.
AI.result: Human-human dialogues exhibit robust syntactic complexity convergence, particularly in task-oriented interactions, whereas human-LLM dialogues show no significant convergence under individual metrics but display a distinct cross-metric pattern under linear-CKA. Classification using syntactic complexity achieves 96% accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Syntactic complexity convergence differs fundamentally between human-human and human-LLM dialogues and provides an effective, likelihood-free signal for LLM dialogue detection.

title: Justification of Emotional Appeal in Computational Argumentation
summary: Emotional appeals (EAs) are often treated as fallacious in computational argumentation, yet they may be justified when warranted by the context. We introduce the task of predicting EA justification and present the first human-annotated dataset for this task, covering 1,176 argument--context pairs. Grounded in philosophical literature, our framework evaluates EA justification along logical and emotional dimensions. Human annotations show that justification criteria form a shared latent judgment space, with evidential proportionality and normative acceptability most strongly associated with overall justification. We further find that EAs without logical support are not always judged fully unjustified, and stronger EAs are not necessarily judged less justified. Finally, LLM experiments show that EA justification prediction remains challenging.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the task of predicting emotional appeal (EA) justification in computational argumentation along with a human-annotated dataset of 1,176 argument-context pairs. Experiments show that EA justification prediction remains challenging for LLMs.
AI.motivation: Computational argumentation often treats emotional appeals as fallacious, overlooking that they can be justified when warranted by the surrounding context.
AI.method: Grounded in philosophical literature, the authors construct a framework evaluating EA justification along logical and emotional dimensions, annotate 1,176 argument-context pairs, and evaluate LLM performance on predicting EA justification.
AI.result: Human annotations reveal a shared latent judgment space where evidential proportionality and normative acceptability most strongly correlate with overall justification; EAs without logical support are not always judged unjustified, and stronger EAs are not necessarily less justified. LLMs struggle to predict EA justification accurately.
AI.conclusion: Predicting whether an emotional appeal is contextually justified is a nuanced, challenging task that opens new directions for computational argumentation.

title: NYUAD at ArGuard Shared Tasks: Multimodal Embedding Models for Detecting Arabic Hateful Memes and Unsafe Prompts
summary: The rapid growth of social media and generative AI has significantly increased the volume of Arabic textual content, memes, and user prompts shared across online platforms. While these media facilitate communication, creativity, and information exchange, they can also be exploited to disseminate hate speech, harmful content, and unsafe instructions. As a result, there is an increasing need for reliable automated methods to identify hateful Arabic memes and harmful (unsafe) prompts. This paper leverages pre-trained and fine-tuned multilingual embedding models to learn rich semantic representations from textual and visual content. The evaluation is conducted using a dataset of Arabic memes and prompts proposed in the ArabicNLP ArGuard 2026 challenge. The results underscore the capacity of large language model (LLM)-based embedding models to deliver superior performance. Developing robust detection systems is essential for improving content moderation and fostering a more secure and trustworthy online environment for Arabic-speaking users.

AI.tldr: This paper presents NYUAD's submission to the ArabicNLP ArGuard 2026 shared tasks, using pre-trained and fine-tuned multilingual embedding models to detect hateful Arabic memes and unsafe prompts. LLM-based embedding models achieve superior detection performance.
AI.motivation: The rapid growth of Arabic social media content and generative AI prompts increases the need for reliable automated moderation of hateful memes and unsafe instructions.
AI.method: The authors leverage pre-trained and fine-tuned multilingual embedding models to extract semantic representations from textual and visual inputs, evaluating them on the ArabicNLP ArGuard 2026 dataset.
AI.result: Experimental results on the ArGuard 2026 challenge demonstrate that LLM-based embedding models deliver superior performance in identifying Arabic hateful memes and unsafe prompts.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal and multilingual LLM-based embeddings provide a strong foundation for improving automated content moderation for Arabic-speaking online platforms.

title: Many Paths to the Same Mistake: Generating Diverse Reasoning Paths Behind the Same Student Mistake
summary: Realistic evaluation of AI systems requires user simulators that capture not only cooperative behavior, but also the errors and variability that arise in real interactions. In educational technology, simulating step-by-step flawed student reasoning is essential, yet datasets mapping these pathways are scarce, and Large Language Models (LLMs) often auto-correct rather than sustain simulated mistakes. To address this, we present a generate-and-filter pipeline that produces diverse and realistic student error traces. Our approach utilizes forward consistency, a metric verifying if a flawed reasoning trace can be used to recover the student's actual incorrect answer, paired with an LLM-as-a-judge to ensure realism. Our evaluation suggests that while many LLMs struggle to maintain incorrect reasoning mid-trace, smaller supervised fine-tuned models successfully capture these divergent paths. This work provides a framework for high-fidelity error trace generation, advancing realistic, non-cooperative user simulation.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a generate-and-filter pipeline to synthesize diverse, realistic step-by-step flawed student reasoning traces for educational user simulation. Smaller supervised fine-tuned models sustain divergent incorrect reasoning better than larger LLMs, which tend to auto-correct.
AI.motivation: Simulating flawed student reasoning is essential for realistic educational AI evaluation, but datasets of error traces are scarce and LLMs often auto-correct mid-trace instead of maintaining the student's mistake.
AI.method: The authors propose a generate-and-filter pipeline that uses forward consistency (verifying whether a flawed trace recovers the student's actual incorrect answer) paired with an LLM-as-a-judge to ensure realism.
AI.result: Evaluations show that many LLMs struggle to sustain incorrect reasoning mid-trace, whereas smaller supervised fine-tuned models successfully capture divergent error pathways.
AI.conclusion: The proposed pipeline enables high-fidelity error trace generation, advancing realistic, non-cooperative user simulation in educational technology.

title: NYUAD at ImageEval Shared Tasks: A Multimodal LLM for Audio-Visual Question Answering and Hallucination Detection in English and Modern Standard Arabic
summary: The increasing adoption of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) has enabled more natural interaction with visual and spoken information, creating new opportunities for intelligent audio-visual question answering (AVQA) and hallucination detection systems. AVQA extends traditional visual question answering by requiring models to jointly understand an input image and a spoken question to generate accurate, context-aware responses. Despite recent advances, AVQA and hallucination detection tasks remain challenging for modern standard Arabic (MSA) due to the limited availability of multimodal datasets and the need to reason across Arabic speech and text modalities alongside visual inputs. In this paper, we present an MLLM-based framework for AVQA that takes an image and a spoken question as input and generates answers. In addition, we utilized this framework to detect hallucination in text-image pairs. The proposed approach is evaluated on the ImageEval 2026 Task (Ayn-VQA) benchmark, which focuses on culturally grounded Arabic AVQA. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively understands spoken queries, grounds their responses in the visual content, and produces accurate answers. The results underscore the capacity and limitations of different LLM architectures for both English and MSA and under various conditions.

AI.tldr: This paper presents NYUAD's MLLM-based framework for the ImageEval 2026 (Ayn-VQA) shared tasks on audio-visual question answering (AVQA) and hallucination detection in English and Modern Standard Arabic (MSA). The framework effectively grounds spoken queries in visual content across both languages.
AI.motivation: AVQA and hallucination detection remain challenging in Modern Standard Arabic due to scarce multimodal datasets and the need to reason jointly across Arabic speech, text, and visual modalities.
AI.method: The authors develop an MLLM-based framework that processes an input image and a spoken question to generate context-aware answers, and apply it to detect hallucinations in text-image pairs on the ImageEval 2026 (Ayn-VQA) benchmark.
AI.result: Experimental results on ImageEval 2026 demonstrate that the proposed framework understands spoken queries and grounds responses accurately in visual content, while highlighting capability differences and limitations across LLM architectures for English and MSA.
AI.conclusion: MLLM-based frameworks can effectively bridge speech, text, and vision for culturally grounded Arabic AVQA and hallucination detection, though architectural limitations remain.

title: Understanding Failures in LLM Reasoning by Learning Structured Representations of Chain-of-Thought
summary: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) is central to improving reasoning in large language models, yet existing evaluation methods focus on step-level signals and ignore the underlying structure of reasoning traces. This raises a key question: what aspects of reasoning quality (i.e., correctness, efficiency, and failure patterns) are encoded in the structure of a CoT trace? We introduce \textbf{CoT2Graph}, a framework that represents CoT traces as directed dependency graphs, making relationships between reasoning steps explicit and capturing patterns such as backtracking, branching, and subtask merging. We model these graphs with graph neural networks and use attribution-based explanations to identify structural patterns associated with reasoning quality. CoT2Graph reveals distinct patterns of successful and failed reasoning: correct CoTs place greater importance on early planning, whereas incorrect CoTs are associated with overloaded synthesis steps and dependency violations. We further show that graph-based signals better predict whether a CoT leads to a correct answer, outperforming previous tree-based structural methods by up to 2.5\% and simple length-based baselines by 7.8\%, while also improving Best-of-$N$ selection. Overall, our results demonstrate that reasoning structure encodes rich signals about reasoning quality, motivating a shift from sequence-level evaluation to structural analysis.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces CoT2Graph, a framework that represents Chain-of-Thought (CoT) traces as directed dependency graphs modeled with graph neural networks to analyze reasoning quality. Graph-based signals outperform tree-based and length-based baselines in predicting CoT correctness and improve Best-of-N selection.
AI.motivation: Existing CoT evaluation methods rely on step-level signals and ignore the structural relationships—such as backtracking, branching, and subtask merging—that encode reasoning quality.
AI.method: CoT2Graph converts CoT traces into directed dependency graphs, models them with graph neural networks, and applies attribution-based explanations to identify structural patterns linked to success and failure.
AI.result: Attribution analysis shows that correct CoTs emphasize early planning while incorrect CoTs exhibit overloaded synthesis steps and dependency violations. CoT2Graph outperforms tree-based structural methods by up to 2.5% and length-based baselines by 7.8% in predicting correctness, and improves Best-of-N selection.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning structure carries rich signals about CoT quality, motivating a shift from sequence-level evaluation to structural graph analysis.

title: When Helpful Agents Cause Financial Harm: Evaluating LLM Agent Safety in Executable Economic Worlds
comment: Accepted (Oral) at EMNLP 2026 Workshop on Financial NLP (FinNLP)
summary: As LLM agents become increasingly capable of making consequential economic decisions, their safety under economic pressures remains poorly understood. We introduce EconSafeBench, the first benchmark for systematically evaluating the safety of LLM agents in executable economic environments. EconSafeBench contains 828 cases across five economic scenarios and four categories of safety violations. A key design is the matched evaluation of three sources of safety pressure, including explicit user requests, pressure from other actors, and pressure arising from the agent's own pursuit of a performance objective. We further evaluate safety at both static and dynamic scales through 30-period interactions with persistent memory and matched controls. Across eight LLMs, all evaluated models exhibit safety violations on the static benchmark, with overall violation rates ranging from 8.5% to 40.6%. We further find that violations can occur even without an explicit unsafe request, and that initially compliant agents may begin to violate as performance pressure increases over time. These findings highlight the need for stronger safety alignment and rigorous evaluation before LLM agents are deployed in high-stakes economic environments.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces EconSafeBench, a benchmark of 828 cases for evaluating LLM agent safety in executable economic environments under static and 30-period dynamic pressures. All eight evaluated LLMs exhibit safety violations, including without explicit unsafe requests.
AI.motivation: As LLM agents make consequential economic decisions, their safety under competing economic pressures—from users, other actors, and their own performance objectives—remains poorly understood.
AI.method: EconSafeBench spans 828 cases across five economic scenarios and four violation categories, testing three matched sources of safety pressure at both static scale and 30-period dynamic interactions with persistent memory.
