AI.result: Across eight evaluated LLMs, static safety violation rates range from 8.5% to 40.6%. Violations occur even without explicit unsafe requests, and initially compliant agents begin violating safety rules as performance pressure accumulates over time.
AI.conclusion: Stronger safety alignment and rigorous dynamic evaluation are needed before deploying LLM agents in high-stakes economic environments.

title: Bridging Semantics and Utilities: A Controllable and Scalable Market Simulation
summary: Large language models(LLMs) have recently been used to construct generative agents for financial market simulation. Existing approaches typically prompt each agent separately with public market information and a private investor profile, and ask the model to directly generate trading actions. In this agent-wise design, the model repeatedly interprets information shared across the population, while individual behavior is controlled through textual descriptions of investor preferences and traits. This creates two structural difficulties: continuous traits such as risk sensitivity do not reliably induce ordered behavioral changes, and repeatedly processing the same public information causes inference costs to grow with the number of agents. We propose \textbf{SUM}, a Semantic-Utility Model that separates cohort-level semantic perception from agent-level utility-based decision-making. A language model interprets public market information for each investor type and produces semantic signals shared within the corresponding cohort. Individual agents then combine these signals with their private states, preferences, and constraints to generate orders through utility-based decisions. Experiments in an A-share limit-order-book market show that \textbf{SUM} provides more stable and monotonic behavioral control than prompt-based agents while substantially reducing repeated language-model inference as the population grows. Closed-loop simulations further reproduce directional market responses, volatility persistence, differentiated investment styles, and persistent wealth heterogeneity. These results establish \textbf{SUM} as a controllable, scalable, and semantically informed framework for financial market simulation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes SUM (Semantic-Utility Model), a financial market simulation framework that separates cohort-level LLM semantic perception from agent-level utility-based decision-making. In an A-share limit-order-book market, SUM provides more stable behavioral control while reducing repeated LLM inference costs.
AI.motivation: Prompting individual LLM agents separately for market simulation causes inference costs to scale with population size and fails to induce reliable, monotonic behavioral changes from continuous traits like risk sensitivity.
AI.method: SUM uses an LLM to interpret public market information once per investor cohort to produce shared semantic signals, which individual agents combine with private states, preferences, and constraints to generate orders via utility-based decisions.
AI.result: Experiments in an A-share limit-order-book market show that SUM achieves more stable and monotonic behavioral control than prompt-based agents while substantially reducing LLM inference. Closed-loop simulations reproduce directional market responses, volatility persistence, differentiated styles, and persistent wealth heterogeneity.
AI.conclusion: Separating cohort-level semantic interpretation from individual utility optimization yields a controllable, scalable framework for LLM-based financial market simulation.

title: Self-Evolving Dual-Role Deliberation for Medication Recommendation from Clinical Records
summary: Recommending medications from electronic health records (EHRs) is a safety-critical task that demands therapeutic coverage, explicit safety constraints, traceable justification, and continual adaptivity. Supervised neural models freeze at deployment and cannot reason about new phenotypes, while existing LLM pipelines are single-pass and lack a cross-case improvement loop. We propose SEMPA, a training-free agentic framework that couples a Proposer with a Critic in multi-round adversarial deliberation, grounds candidates with molecular-aware retrieval, contrastively evolves both agents' natural-language policies under a semantic-anchor constraint, and enforces rule-based DDI and contraindication checks. On 100 MIMIC-IV encounters, SEMPA reaches 0.3116 Jaccard, 0.7295 F1, and a 0.0172 DDI rate, improving F1 by 57.7% and cutting DDI by 77.5% over the strongest supervised baseline. Two LLM judges rank SEMPA highest, and six-backbone studies confirm that gains derive from the framework rather than a specific model.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes SEMPA, a training-free agentic framework for medication recommendation from EHRs using dual-role Proposer-Critic deliberation, molecular-aware retrieval, and rule-based safety checks. On MIMIC-IV, SEMPA improves F1 by 57.7% and cuts drug-drug interaction (DDI) rates by 77.5% over the strongest supervised baseline.
AI.motivation: Supervised neural models for medication recommendation freeze at deployment and cannot adapt to new phenotypes, while existing single-pass LLM pipelines lack cross-case improvement loops and explicit safety enforcement.
AI.method: SEMPA couples a Proposer and Critic in multi-round adversarial deliberation, grounds candidates via molecular-aware retrieval, contrastively evolves both agents' natural-language policies under a semantic-anchor constraint, and enforces rule-based DDI and contraindication checks.
AI.result: On 100 MIMIC-IV encounters, SEMPA achieves 0.3116 Jaccard, 0.7295 F1, and a 0.0172 DDI rate, improving F1 by 57.7% and reducing DDI by 77.5% over the strongest supervised baseline. Two LLM judges rank SEMPA highest, and six-backbone studies confirm the gains stem from the framework.
AI.conclusion: Training-free dual-role deliberation with policy evolution and explicit safety checks offers an accurate, adaptable, and safer paradigm for clinical medication recommendation.

title: The Judge Is Not Impartial: Self-Preference in Medical LLM Evaluation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to evaluate model-generated medical content, creating a potential circularity: an LLM judge may favor outputs generated by the same model independently of clinical quality. To characterize LLM judge self-preference in medical settings, we measured same-model affinity in single-turn specialist question answering and multi-turn standardized-patient encounters. We evaluated eight models, two from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Qwen, on 620 real point of care questions from clinicians (Real-POCQi). The same eight models also generated and judged 200 standardized patient-clinician scenarios (MedSP1000) up to 8 visible turns. In total, our analysis spans 13,760 LLM judgments. We define three complementary measures of self-preference. Answer Rank Bias, our primary measure, compared the rank assigned to a fixed response by its own-model judge with its average rank from outside judges. Answer Score Bias made the analogous comparison using rubric scores. Own-Answer Win Rate measured how often a judge ranked its own model's response above a competitor. Higher values across all these measures indicate greater degrees of self-preference. In Real-POCQi, pooled Answer Rank Bias was $+1.22$ positions, and all eight judges favored their own answers. Self-preference persisted both with and without a grading rubric. Revealing generator identities modestly weakened self-preference by an average of $-0.094$ positions. In MedSP1000, pooled Answer Rank Bias ranged from $+0.53$ to $+0.62$ positions, with no clear difference by conversation length ($p=0.17$). LLM judges systematically favored responses generated by their own models across multiple formats. Clinical AI deployments should exercise increased vigilance including multiple evaluation measures and judge panels spanning differing model families when deploying LLM-as-a-judge systems.

AI.tldr: This study measures LLM judge self-preference across eight models from four families on 620 clinical questions (Real-POCQi) and 200 standardized-patient scenarios (MedSP1000). LLM judges systematically favor their own models' responses across both single-turn and multi-turn medical formats.
AI.motivation: Using LLMs to evaluate medical content risks circularity if judges favor outputs from their own model regardless of clinical quality.
AI.method: The authors evaluate eight models (two each from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Qwen) across 13,760 judgments using three measures—Answer Rank Bias, Answer Score Bias, and Own-Answer Win Rate—while testing the effects of grading rubrics and revealing generator identities.
AI.result: On Real-POCQi, pooled Answer Rank Bias is +1.22 positions, with all eight judges favoring their own answers; self-preference persists with or without a rubric and is only modestly reduced (-0.094 positions) by revealing identities. On MedSP1000, pooled Answer Rank Bias ranges from +0.53 to +0.62 positions regardless of conversation length (p = 0.17).
AI.conclusion: Clinical AI deployments using LLM-as-a-judge should employ multiple evaluation measures and diverse judge panels spanning different model families to mitigate self-preference bias.

title: Intrinsic Attention as Navigator: A Non-Generative Retrieval Method for Multi-Hop Queries
summary: For multi-hop queries in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), it is crucial to accurately obtain evidence pieces. In this study, we propose a training-free method for multi-hop query retrieval, named Intrinsic Navigating-based Non-Generative Retrieval (IN-Retriever). Instead of generating intermediate reasoning text, the method extracts the bridging clue from the internal attention of the embedding model based on the current context and retrieved candidate documents. During iterative clue extraction and document retrieval, IN-Retriever strips away revealed clues from the embedded query vector and then reranks candidate documents in a targeted manner, thereby steering retrieval toward hidden next-hop evidence. In the experiments, we confirm the feasibility and effectiveness of using intrinsic attention signals to guide external multi-hop retrieval. Experimental results show that our method precisely collects sufficient documents to support multi-hop queries and significantly outperforms sparse and dense retrieval methods.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes IN-Retriever, a training-free multi-hop retrieval method that uses internal attention from an embedding model to extract bridging clues and steer iterative retrieval without generating intermediate text. It significantly outperforms sparse and dense retrieval baselines on multi-hop queries.
AI.motivation: Multi-hop RAG queries require accurately retrieving sequential evidence pieces, which standard sparse/dense retrievers struggle with and generative query-rewriting methods address at higher cost.
AI.method: IN-Retriever extracts bridging clues from the embedding model's internal attention over the current context and retrieved candidates, strips revealed clues from the embedded query vector, and reranks candidate documents to target hidden next-hop evidence.
AI.result: Experiments confirm that intrinsic attention signals effectively guide external multi-hop retrieval, with IN-Retriever collecting sufficient supporting documents and significantly outperforming sparse and dense retrieval methods.
AI.conclusion: Intrinsic attention in embedding models provides an effective, non-generative navigation signal for multi-hop RAG retrieval.

title: Assisting Patients with Reliable Information Gathering: A Guide to Building Efficient QA Systems for Medical Use
summary: The application of question-answering (QA) systems in the medical domain has rapidly advanced, significantly improving patients' access to reliable health-related information. However, current approaches face notable challenges, including the difficulty in obtaining large-scale and unbiased medical datasets, significant privacy concerns, and inefficiencies due to manual dataset annotation. To address these issues, This study introduce a novel methodology leveraging publicly accessible online health forums to systematically build an unbiased, privacy-conscious QA dataset, and it employs Topic-guided Semantic Modeling (TGSM) for automated topic identification, enabling efficient and targeted annotation of relevant patient-generated content. Subsequently, this study propose a two-stage QA pipeline based on a Retriever-Reader architecture, which is further enhanced through fine-tuning state-of-the-art transformer-based models on the constructed domain-specific QA dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that our fine-tuned BioBERT significantly outperforms existing benchmarks, offering accurate patient-derived insights and providing a replicable framework for building efficient medical QA systems.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a methodology for building an unbiased, privacy-conscious medical QA dataset from online health forums using Topic-guided Semantic Modeling (TGSM) and fine-tuning BioBERT in a Retriever-Reader pipeline. The fine-tuned BioBERT outperforms existing benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Medical QA systems face challenges in acquiring large-scale, unbiased datasets due to privacy concerns and the inefficiency of manual annotation.
AI.method: The authors extract patient-generated content from public online health forums, apply Topic-guided Semantic Modeling (TGSM) for automated topic identification and targeted annotation, and fine-tune transformer models (including BioBERT) within a two-stage Retriever-Reader QA pipeline.
AI.result: Experimental results show that the fine-tuned BioBERT significantly outperforms existing benchmarks in delivering accurate patient-derived health insights.
AI.conclusion: Combining forum-derived data with TGSM-guided annotation provides a replicable, privacy-conscious framework for building efficient medical QA systems.

title: CondRelBench: A Mixed-Domain Benchmark for Condition-Scoped Relation Understanding
comment: 37 pages, 2 figures, 28 tables. Code and data are available online
summary: Relation extraction systems often identify what a relation is, but not the condition under which it holds. This can collapse condition-bound claims into unsupported generalizations, a failure we call relation overgeneralization. We introduce CondRelBench, a mixed-domain benchmark for evaluating condition-scoped relation understanding. Each claim is represented as (E1, R, E2 | C), where C is the condition licensing the relation. Using 3,000 synthetic paragraphs, 200 PubMed full-text papers, and 695 Reddit posts, we construct five probe variants per tuple that preserve, replace, remove, or contradict the condition, or contradict the relation itself. Models classify each probe as Supported, Not Supported, or Not Enough Evidence. We also introduce Overgeneralization Rate (OGR) and Scope Preservation Score (SPS) to measure false support for altered claims and consistency across probe families. Across prompted LLMs, fine-tuned LLMs, and encoder models, we find that Accuracy and Macro F1 often hide scope failures. Models frequently support the original scoped claim but fail when its condition is removed or altered. Domain-specific encoders achieve the strongest scope preservation, while instruction-tuned LLMs often show higher overgeneralization. Synthetic supervision helps but does not close the gap to real-world PubMed and Reddit performance.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces CondRelBench, a mixed-domain benchmark for condition-scoped relation understanding, along with Overgeneralization Rate (OGR) and Scope Preservation Score (SPS) metrics. Evaluations show that high Accuracy and Macro F1 often mask scope failures, especially in instruction-tuned LLMs.
AI.motivation: Relation extraction systems frequently identify a relation without capturing the condition under which it holds, collapsing condition-bound claims into unsupported generalizations (relation overgeneralization).
AI.method: Representing claims as (E1, R, E2 | C), the authors construct five probe variants (preserving, replacing, removing, or contradicting the condition, or contradicting the relation) across 3,000 synthetic paragraphs, 200 PubMed papers, and 695 Reddit posts, evaluating prompted LLMs, fine-tuned LLMs, and encoder models with OGR and SPS.
AI.result: Models often support original scoped claims but fail when conditions are removed or altered, which standard Accuracy and Macro F1 hide. Domain-specific encoders achieve the strongest scope preservation, while instruction-tuned LLMs exhibit higher overgeneralization, and synthetic supervision does not fully close the gap to real-world PubMed and Reddit data.
AI.conclusion: Evaluating condition-scoped relation understanding requires dedicated scope-sensitive metrics and mixed-domain benchmarks like CondRelBench.

title: Which Mathematical Context Supports Target-Aligned Conjecture Generation? A Paired Ablation Study
comment: 16 pages, 2 figures, 6 tables. To appear in the Proceedings of the 4th Workshop on Mathematical Natural Language Processing (MathNLP 2026)
summary: Generating mathematical conjectures from natural-language context is challenging because theorem-relevant information is distributed across multiple forms of mathematical context, including definitions, objects, assumptions, and constructions. We study which of these contextual signals help a model recover the specific claim supported by the surrounding setup, using 61 main theorems from 12 papers across four mathematical domains. For each theorem, we redact the result and represent the remaining setup using six context components. A paired ablation design compares full context, six leave-one-out conditions, and six single-component conditions, yielding 793 generated conjectures. Context components were largely complementary: removing one component usually had little effect, whereas retaining only one substantially reduced expected-theorem alignment. Local Mathematical Objects provided the strongest standalone signal, while Structural Constraints and Conditions produced the largest alignment decrease when removed. These findings suggest that target-aligned conjecture generation depends on combining information that identifies relevant objects with information that constrains admissible claims.

AI.tldr: This study conducts a paired ablation across 61 theorems from 12 math papers to determine which mathematical context components support target-aligned conjecture generation. Local Mathematical Objects provide the strongest standalone signal, while removing Structural Constraints and Conditions causes the largest alignment drop.
AI.motivation: Generating mathematical conjectures from natural-language context is difficult because theorem-relevant information is spread across definitions, objects, assumptions, and constructions, and their relative contributions are unclear.
AI.method: Using 61 main theorems across four mathematical domains, the authors redact each theorem's result, represent the setup using six context components, and run a paired ablation comparing full context, leave-one-out, and single-component conditions (yielding 793 generated conjectures).
AI.result: Context components are largely complementary: removing one component has little effect, whereas retaining only one substantially reduces alignment with the expected theorem. Local Mathematical Objects give the strongest standalone signal, while removing Structural Constraints and Conditions causes the largest alignment decrease.
AI.conclusion: Target-aligned conjecture generation relies on combining context that identifies relevant mathematical objects with constraints that bound admissible claims.

title: RGFC: Registry Grounded Function Calling with stage-decomposed evaluation
comment: 39 pages, 17 figures, 17 tables. Contains link to a dataset hosted on huggingface
summary: Tool-calling evaluations often report whether the final call matches a reference answer, but this single outcome merges different failures: choosing a function outside the available registry, violating the selected schema, or filling arguments with values not supported by the user request. These failures matter more when models must choose from larger tool registries. We introduce RFCD, a registry-scaled function-calling benchmark built from BFCL, Glaive Function Calling v2, and Tool-Call-Data, with standardized JSON-schema registries ranging from 5 to 3,000 functions. We also introduce TAAG, a deterministic stage-decomposed evaluator for registry conformance, structural completeness, and argument grounding. Across six locally served sub-4B models, three data sources, and four feedback modes, registry scale is the dominant source of degradation: single-pass TAAG pass rate drops sharply from small to large registries on all sources. Repeated feedback improves some grounding metrics but adds substantial token cost and does not consistently improve end-to-end F1. Requirement-level TAAG-R feedback gives modest gains over stage-only TAAG-S feedback, which indicates that TAAG signals are useful for analysis and correction probes but do not solve registry scaling by themselves. RFCD and TAAG provide an evaluation resource for measuring where tool-calling systems fail as registries grow.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces RFCD, a registry-scaled function-calling benchmark (5 to 3,000 functions), and TAAG, a stage-decomposed evaluator for registry conformance, structural completeness, and argument grounding. Across six sub-4B models, registry scale is the dominant driver of performance degradation.
AI.motivation: Standard tool-calling evaluations report only final call match, conflating distinct failures—out-of-registry selection, schema violations, and ungrounded arguments—that worsen as tool registries grow.
AI.method: The authors build RFCD from BFCL, Glaive Function Calling v2, and Tool-Call-Data with standardized JSON-schema registries of 5 to 3,000 functions, and evaluate six locally served sub-4B models across four feedback modes using the deterministic TAAG evaluator.
AI.result: Single-pass TAAG pass rates drop sharply from small to large registries across all sources. Repeated feedback improves some grounding metrics at substantial token cost without consistently improving end-to-end F1, and requirement-level TAAG-R feedback yields only modest gains over stage-only TAAG-S feedback.
AI.conclusion: RFCD and TAAG expose where small tool-calling models fail as registries scale, showing that decomposed feedback alone does not resolve registry-scaling bottlenecks.

title: Evaluating the Robustness of Fact-Checking LLMs on Multilingual Evidence
comment: 13 pages, 16 figures Accepted at COLM Sci-FM 2026
summary: Automated fact-checking benchmarks typically pair claims with clean, curated evidence in high-resource languages, but real-world evidence is often incomplete, misleading, or written in a language where models are weaker. We evaluate the robustness of fact-checking LLMs for different languages. Building on EuroVerdict, we construct gold evidence sets for 190 claims in each of English, German, Greek, and Romanian, then apply four corruption strategies at two severity levels. We test LLMs on a set of claims, providing them with evidence from the sets above. A rubric-based LLM-as-a-judge scores reasoning quality. Verdict accuracy proves highly sensitive to both factors: Misleading edit cut Llama 3.1 8B's English accuracy from 80.00% to 16.84%, and losses widen as language resource level decreases. Machine-translating Greek and Romanian claims into English recovers much, but not all, of the low-resource gap. Judge scores decline more slowly than accuracy, suggesting that automated reasoning evaluation underestimates degradation. These results caution against deploying LLM fact-checkers on noisy multilingual evidence, and we release our evidence datasets and evaluation code to support future work.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates the robustness of fact-checking LLMs across English, German, Greek, and Romanian under four evidence corruption strategies. Verdict accuracy drops sharply under misleading edits and in lower-resource languages, while LLM-as-a-judge reasoning scores underestimate this degradation.
AI.motivation: Automated fact-checking benchmarks typically use clean, high-resource English evidence, leaving LLM robustness on noisy, incomplete, or low-resource multilingual evidence unmeasured.
AI.method: Building on EuroVerdict, the authors construct gold evidence sets for 190 claims in each of four languages, apply four corruption strategies at two severity levels, and evaluate LLMs alongside a rubric-based LLM-as-a-judge for reasoning quality.
AI.result: Misleading edits cut Llama 3.1 8B's English verdict accuracy from 80.00% to 16.84%, with larger losses in lower-resource languages. Machine-translating Greek and Romanian claims into English recovers most but not all of the gap, while judge reasoning scores decline more slowly than verdict accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Deploying LLM fact-checkers on noisy multilingual evidence carries significant reliability risks, and automated reasoning judges can mask severe verdict degradation.

title: Skill Transfer: Adapting Agent Skills from Strong to Weak Agents
summary: Agent skills are modular bundles of instructions, code, and resources that an agent loads on demand, increasingly authored and validated on frontier models and shared as an open standard. The same skill behaves differently across models: a strong model turns it into a large performance gain, while a weak model realizes little of that gain and sometimes does worse than with no skill at all. Cost and resource constraints, however, often restrict real deployments to exactly these weaker agents. We hypothesize that the strong model silently supplies procedural steps the skill leaves implicit, which the weak model omits, and formalize closing this gap as \emph{Skill Transfer}: holding the skill's capability ceiling and the model's parameters fixed, we adapt the skill so a specific weak agent can execute it well. Our method abstracts strong and weak trajectories into typed execution structures, localizes their structural divergence with a graph edit distance (GED), and repairs the skill through an iterative diagnoser-patcher loop. Across three benchmarks and two model families, Skill Transfer raises pass rate over the unmodified skill significantly and well over other skill-evolution baselines. The adapted skill also improves the strong agent it was never adapted for, and transfers out of distribution to a structurally related, unseen task. Code is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes Skill Transfer—adapting modular agent skills so weak models can execute them effectively—by abstracting strong and weak trajectories, localizing divergence via graph edit distance (GED), and repairing skills in a diagnoser-patcher loop. Skill Transfer significantly boosts pass rates across three benchmarks and two model families.
AI.motivation: Agent skills authored on frontier models often fail on weaker, cost-constrained models because strong models silently supply implicit procedural steps that weak models omit.
AI.method: Holding the skill's capability ceiling and model parameters fixed, the method abstracts strong and weak execution trajectories into typed structures, localizes structural divergence using GED, and iteratively repairs the skill via a diagnoser-patcher loop.
AI.result: Across three benchmarks and two model families, Skill Transfer significantly increases pass rates over unmodified skills and outperforms skill-evolution baselines. The adapted skills also improve the strong agent and transfer out-of-distribution to a related unseen task.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly surfacing and patching implicit procedural steps enables reliable transfer of agent skills from strong to weak models.

title: Interpretability-Guided Auditing for Clinical Language Models for Discharge Prediction
summary: Clinical natural language processing (NLP) models for hospital discharge prediction are vulnerable to explicit discharge-related lexical cues in clinical notes, even when note timestamps are temporally filtered. These cues may act as proxies for future outcomes, leading models to rely on shortcut-like signals rather than clinically meaningful evidence. We propose AuditBERT-Discharge, a lightweight framework that reframes interpretability as a training-time auditing mechanism. Token-level SHAP attributions from an initial BioClinicalBERT model are used to identify highly attributed discharge-related tokens, which are subsequently masked in the training corpus before model retraining. We evaluate the framework on a retrospective cohort of elective spine surgery encounters from a single academic medical center. Qualitative attribution analysis and preliminary evaluation suggest that SHAP-guided auditing reduces reliance on explicit discharge-proxy language and yields more conservative, better-calibrated predictions, although improvements in discrimination are not uniform. These findings demonstrate the potential of interpretability-guided auditing as a practical strategy for identifying and constraining shortcut-like lexical dependencies in temporally sensitive clinical NLP tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes AuditBERT-Discharge, a training-time auditing framework that uses token-level SHAP attributions from BioClinicalBERT to mask explicit discharge-proxy tokens before retraining. Preliminary evaluation on elective spine surgery encounters shows reduced reliance on lexical shortcuts and better-calibrated predictions.
AI.motivation: Clinical NLP models for hospital discharge prediction exploit explicit discharge-related lexical cues as future-outcome proxies, even after temporal filtering of clinical notes.
AI.method: AuditBERT-Discharge computes token-level SHAP attributions from an initial BioClinicalBERT model, identifies highly attributed discharge-related tokens, masks them in the training corpus, and retrains the model.
AI.result: On a retrospective cohort of elective spine surgery encounters, qualitative attribution analysis and preliminary evaluation indicate that SHAP-guided auditing reduces reliance on discharge-proxy language and yields more conservative, better-calibrated predictions, though discrimination gains are not uniform.
AI.conclusion: Interpretability-guided auditing offers a practical, lightweight mechanism to constrain lexical shortcuts in temporally sensitive clinical NLP tasks.

title: FlashREINFORCE: Critic-Free Single-Rollout Asynchronous RL for Agentic Language Models
summary: Asynchronous reinforcement learning suits long-horizon agents with irregular rollout times, but group-relative updates require repeated rollouts of each prompt. However, group-based sampling limits prompt coverage at a fixed rollout budget and introduces group synchronization barriers. One rollout per prompt avoids these constraints but removes the variance-reducing group baseline, making updates noisier and more prone to instability on stale, variable-length trajectories. We present FlashREINFORCE, a critic-free, one-pass framework built on One-Batch REINFORCE, a Sequence Trust Region, and Sample-Mean Optimization. These components preserve prompt coverage and signed feedback while controlling policy drift and length-amplified negative updates. In our experiments, FlashREINFORCE remains stable through 6,000 updates on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B at a policy lag of approximately four updates. On Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, it reaches 38.0 mean accuracy across five benchmarks, outperforming the reported GRPO baseline by 1.7 percentage points with half the rollouts (256k versus 512k). Python-tool experiments extend to the 30B MoE model Qwen3-30B-A3B, with stable training at policy lag eight. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, FlashREINFORCE maintains tool use where GRPO stops making tool calls and achieves 98.3%/96.5% seen/unseen ALFWorld success.

AI.tldr: This paper presents FlashREINFORCE, a critic-free, single-rollout asynchronous RL framework for agentic LLMs built on One-Batch REINFORCE, a Sequence Trust Region, and Sample-Mean Optimization. It outperforms GRPO on math benchmarks with half the rollouts and maintains stable tool use on ALFWorld.
AI.motivation: Group-relative asynchronous RL (like GRPO) requires repeated rollouts per prompt, limiting prompt coverage and creating synchronization barriers, whereas single-rollout methods suffer from high variance and instability on stale, variable-length trajectories.
AI.method: FlashREINFORCE combines One-Batch REINFORCE, a Sequence Trust Region, and Sample-Mean Optimization to preserve prompt coverage and signed feedback while controlling policy drift and length-amplified negative updates.
AI.result: FlashREINFORCE remains stable through 6,000 updates on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B at policy lag ~4 and scales stably to Qwen3-30B-A3B at lag 8. On Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, it reaches 38.0 mean accuracy across five benchmarks (outperforming GRPO by 1.7 points with 256k vs. 512k rollouts), and on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct it preserves tool use where GRPO collapses, achieving 98.3%/96.5% seen/unseen ALFWorld success.
AI.conclusion: Critic-free single-rollout asynchronous RL with sequence trust-region control enables stable, sample-efficient agentic LLM training.

title: EmoTrace: Recursive Trace-Factorized Generation for Emotional Support Conversation
summary: Fundamental to effective emotional support is the iterative interpersonal dynamic wherein a supporter intervention continuously shapes the psychological trajectory of the seeker. While contemporary models capture variables at the turn level, including transient emotions and discrete strategies, they inherently treat these factors as isolated events. By retaining strictly literal dialogue histories while discarding the underlying decision logic, such architectures remain fundamentally incapable of sustaining coherent extended support. Here we introduce EmoTrace, a recursive method utilizing trace factorization to preserve explicit decision continuity throughout interactions spanning multiple turns. Departing from others, our approach formulates each conversational turn as a structured interaction increment encapsulating the evolving state of the seeker, the selected strategy, the affect of the supporter, and the ultimate textual realization. Accumulated sequentially, this trajectory of increments functions as an explicit structural trace informing subsequent interventions. Optimization of this factorized generation is achieved through two complementary mechanisms. Specifically, a value guidance mechanism aligns discrete factor selection with interaction values over an extended horizon, whereas a trace conditioning mechanism refines textual realization contingent upon the fixed strategic trace. Empirical evaluations across standard benchmarks demonstrate that EmoTrace yields substantial improvements in both strategic planning and response generation. Crucially, rollouts spanning multiple turns reveal that these retained structural traces confer compounding benefits over extended dialogues, establishing a robust mechanism for sustained affective alignment in human-machine interaction.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces EmoTrace, a recursive trace-factorized generation method for emotional support conversations that preserves explicit decision continuity across turns. Evaluations show substantial gains in strategic planning and response generation, with compounding benefits over extended dialogues.
AI.motivation: Existing emotional support models treat emotions and strategies at the isolated turn level and retain only literal dialogue history, losing the underlying decision logic needed for coherent multi-turn support.
AI.method: EmoTrace formulates each turn as a structured interaction increment (seeker state, selected strategy, supporter affect, and textual realization) accumulated into an explicit structural trace, optimized via value guidance for discrete factor selection and trace conditioning for response realization.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations on standard benchmarks demonstrate substantial improvements in both strategic planning and response generation, with multi-turn rollouts showing compounding benefits over extended dialogues.
AI.conclusion: Retaining explicit, factorized decision traces provides a robust mechanism for sustained affective alignment in multi-turn emotional support conversations.

title: Decision 1.0: Towards Open Decision Foundation Models
summary: Intelligent software needs reusable judgments inside its control flow: selecting an action, testing a condition, or assessing evidence against a rubric. We present Decision 1.0, an open-weight family that turns textual state and runtime-defined questions into typed probability distributions. Its Choice, Noul, and Score interface lets applications specify outcomes at inference time and compose predictions into agents and workflows. Each question produces its candidate distribution without autoregressive text generation. Six models cover bidirectional encoder and causal decoder architectures, including a workflow specialist. Training draws on verifiable tasks, natural-language annotations, and workflow adaptation. On a common decision benchmark, Lux-9B achieves 84.17\% on explicit decisions and 91.25\% on inference, with a weighted overall score of 77.22\%. Results also expose gaps in composition, transfer, and probability calibration. Released weights and inference code provide a basis for developing decision models as reusable components of software.

AI.tldr: This paper presents Decision 1.0, a family of six open-weight decision foundation models that convert textual state and runtime-defined questions into typed probability distributions without autoregressive generation. Lux-9B achieves 77.22% weighted overall score on a common decision benchmark.
AI.motivation: Intelligent software needs reusable, non-autoregressive judgments (selecting actions, testing conditions, scoring evidence) integrated directly into control flow.
AI.method: Decision 1.0 provides a Choice, Noul, and Score interface across six encoder, decoder, and workflow-specialist models trained on verifiable tasks, natural-language annotations, and workflow adaptation.
AI.result: On a common decision benchmark, Lux-9B achieves 84.17% on explicit decisions, 91.25% on inference, and a 77.22% weighted overall score, while also revealing gaps in composition, transfer, and probability calibration.
AI.conclusion: Released weights and inference code establish a foundation for treating decision models as reusable software components.

title: All the Pieces Matter! A Six-stage Analysis of an Underground Fraud Ecosystem on Dread
summary: Cyber-enabled fraud is a dominant global threat that causes severe financial loss, identity theft, and widespread psychological harm. This illicit economy relies on a highly specialized underground ecosystem where distinct actors exchange technical tools, operational techniques, and laundering channels. This research presents a case study of one such live fraud ecosystem from the perspective of a cohesive six-stage value chain spanning from preparation to monetization: Capability, Data Acquisition, Technique Sharing, Identity Forgery, Execution, and Extraction. Analyzing 67,976 posts and 305,048 comments from nine communities on the Tor-based darknet forum Dread, we map user trajectories, content distribution, and the adoption of generative AI. Our findings show that structural cohesion within the ecosystem is maintained by a thin layer of `bridgers' who generate the majority of all content. Against a degree-preserving null model, three knowledge-building upstream stages of the value chain form a tightly coupled cluster, whereas the remaining three operational downstream stages resolve into highly specialized populations with small personnel overlap. Finally, we demonstrate that generative AI is being rapidly but unevenly absorbed across the value chain; the technology saturates knowledge-building communities while operational stages remain largely untouched. By quantifying criminal specialization and structural integration, our network-based approach provides a framework for targeted, high-impact law enforcement interventions.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes 67,976 posts and 305,048 comments from the darknet forum Dread to map an underground fraud ecosystem across a six-stage value chain. It finds that a thin layer of bridgers maintains cohesion, upstream stages cluster tightly, and generative AI saturates knowledge-building stages but not operational ones.
AI.motivation: Cyber-enabled fraud relies on a specialized underground ecosystem, yet its structural integration, actor trajectories, and uneven adoption of generative AI across operational stages remain poorly quantified.
AI.method: The authors analyze 67,976 posts and 305,048 comments across nine Dread communities using a six-stage value chain (Capability, Data Acquisition, Technique Sharing, Identity Forgery, Execution, Extraction) and compare structural cohesion against a degree-preserving null model.
AI.result: A thin layer of bridgers generates most content and maintains cohesion; three upstream knowledge-building stages form a tightly coupled cluster, whereas three downstream operational stages consist of specialized populations with little overlap. Generative AI saturates upstream knowledge-building communities while operational stages remain largely untouched.
AI.conclusion: Quantifying criminal specialization and structural integration across the fraud value chain provides a framework for targeted law enforcement interventions.

title: Beyond Binary Audits: Does Guideline Grounding Mitigate Decision-Space Framing in LLM Opioid Prescribing?
summary: Audits of LLMs for bias in opioid prescribing have largely relied on binary treatment decisions, a signal that current models have saturated. We introduce Q-Pain++, a full-factorial stress test that holds clinical content fixed while independently varying clinical risk factors and the granularity of the available dosage options. Adding an intermediate dosage option to otherwise unchanged vignettes substantially lowers agreement with expert-annotated dosages for most models, while demographic differences in dosage decisions remain small in all but one configuration once clinical risk factors are added. Grounding models in perioperative guidelines through retrieval reduces this framing effect on average but does not eliminate it, and one model's treatment decisions change when the retrieved passages are reordered. These results suggest that audits should vary the answer format, not only patient identity. We will release our codebase as well as Guideline-RAG-associated resources on GitHub (this https URL).

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Q-Pain++, a full-factorial stress test for LLM opioid prescribing that varies clinical risk factors and dosage option granularity. Adding an intermediate dosage option substantially lowers expert agreement, and guideline RAG reduces but does not eliminate this framing effect.
AI.motivation: Binary treatment audits of LLM prescribing bias have saturated, leaving sensitivity to decision-space framing and clinical risk factors unexamined.
AI.method: Q-Pain++ holds clinical content fixed while independently varying clinical risk factors and dosage option granularity, and evaluates the mitigating effect of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) grounded in perioperative guidelines.
AI.result: Adding an intermediate dosage option substantially reduces agreement with expert-annotated dosages for most models, while demographic differences remain small in all but one configuration once risk factors are included. Guideline RAG reduces this framing effect on average without eliminating it, and reordering retrieved passages alters one model's decisions.
AI.conclusion: Clinical LLM audits should vary answer formats and decision-space granularity, not just patient identity.

title: ReVision: Selective Intrinsic Reasoning for Tool-Augmented, Reasoning-Intensive VQA
summary: External tools substantially expand what multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can retrieve and compute on reasoning-intensive visual questions, and aggregate accuracy typically improves when tools are available. Our empirical study across six VQA benchmarks shows that aggregate accuracy gains under tool access can coexist with answer reversals: questions answered correctly without tools but incorrectly with tools. Trajectory analysis reveals substantially shorter reasoning turns under tool access, suggesting a shift from intrinsic visual reasoning toward reliance on external outputs. We propose ReVision, a training-free test-time method that registers intrinsic reconsideration as an optional action alongside search and code execution. When invoked, a separate tool-free multimodal call re-examines the original image, integrates accumulated evidence, and returns a revised analysis. The MLLM chooses if and when to use it, without fixed reflection stages or paired rollouts. ReVision improves over standard tool use on all six benchmarks (1.28--7.51\%) and outperforms Dual-Rollout Combine on five, with reasoning-token use comparable to standard tool use.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes ReVision, a training-free test-time method that registers intrinsic visual reconsideration as an optional tool-free action for tool-augmented MLLMs. ReVision improves over standard tool use on all six VQA benchmarks by 1.28% to 7.51%.
AI.motivation: Tool-augmented MLLMs achieve higher aggregate VQA accuracy but suffer answer reversals—failing questions they previously answered correctly without tools—because shorter reasoning turns shift reliance from intrinsic visual reasoning to external tool outputs.
AI.method: ReVision adds intrinsic reconsideration as an optional action alongside search and code execution; when invoked, a separate tool-free multimodal call re-examines the original image, integrates accumulated evidence, and returns a revised analysis without fixed reflection stages or paired rollouts.
AI.result: ReVision outperforms standard tool use on all six VQA benchmarks (by 1.28% to 7.51%) and beats Dual-Rollout Combine on five benchmarks, while keeping reasoning-token usage comparable to standard tool use.
AI.conclusion: Allowing MLLMs to selectively invoke tool-free visual reconsideration mitigates tool-induced answer reversals efficiently at test time.

title: Winning the Leaderboard, Losing the Distribution: Diagnosing and Mitigating Acoustic Narrowing in Low-Resource ASR
comment: 29 pages, 12 figures. Code, per-utterance outputs and fact ledger: this https URL
summary: For a low-resource language, one public leaderboard is often the only shared measure of progress, so optimizing toward it means optimizing toward a test distribution. Our low-rank fine-tune of whisper-large-v3-turbo ranked first on MediaSpeech, Common Voice 17 and a five-set Turkish community board, at 9.02% word error on MediaSpeech against 11.93% for the best baseline. On its private split it lost to unmodified whisper-large-v3. We treat that split as an alarm, not evidence; the main finding does not depend on it. On a twenty-condition FLEURS-TR benchmark built independently of our model selection, the unmodified base beats every fine-tune in every condition, and all five deficits clear zero under paired bootstrap. We call this acoustic narrowing: fine-tuning contracts the acoustic range a model serves well. The central finding is methodological: our in-house proxy for detecting narrowing concealed it instead, ranking the narrowed fine-tune above the sturdier base. Model selection needs a proxy from an independently produced distribution; more of the same source will not do. A rebuilt pipeline reduces the narrowing: a larger mixture with disclosed provenance, a higher-capacity base, and base-referenced selection with trajectory averaging. It wins three same-provenance axes and draws level on FLEURS-TR, 8.16% against 8.26%, interval spanning zero. Parity holds under a second inference stack and a full epoch, decoder fixed. The recovery is one trajectory, a demonstration rather than a validated recipe. In Kazakh the inversion reappears on corpora we did not build. With matched trainable-parameter shares, fine-tuning raised out-of-pool error by 2.23 points for an attention encoder-decoder and lowered it by 3.46 for a CTC encoder-only model, across three seeds each. Narrowing thus depends on the system adapted. We release TurkSpeak Bench, a robustness-first Turkish ASR leaderboard.

AI.tldr: This paper diagnoses "acoustic narrowing" in low-resource ASR, where fine-tuning whisper-large-v3-turbo wins public Turkish leaderboards (9.02% WER on MediaSpeech) but degrades on an independent 20-condition FLEURS-TR benchmark. A rebuilt pipeline with a higher-capacity base and base-referenced selection mitigates the narrowing.
AI.motivation: Optimizing low-resource ASR for a single public leaderboard risks overfitting to its test distribution, while same-source in-house proxies can conceal resulting out-of-distribution degradation.
AI.method: The authors evaluate fine-tuned models on an independent 20-condition FLEURS-TR benchmark, rebuild the pipeline using a larger disclosed mixture, a higher-capacity base, and base-referenced selection with trajectory averaging, and test cross-architecture behavior on Kazakh.
AI.result: Unmodified whisper-large-v3 beats every fine-tune across all 20 FLEURS-TR conditions, whereas the rebuilt pipeline draws level on FLEURS-TR (8.16% vs. 8.26%) while winning three same-provenance axes. In Kazakh, fine-tuning raises out-of-pool error by 2.23 points for an attention encoder-decoder but lowers it by 3.46 points for a CTC encoder-only model.
AI.conclusion: Model selection requires proxies from independently produced distributions, and the authors release TurkSpeak Bench as a robustness-first Turkish ASR leaderboard.

title: Non-Deterministic Finite Automata for Telugu Letters and Visualizations for Metrical Poetry
summary: Syllabic weight is central to Telugu metrical poetry. Syllabically, every letter (aksharam token) is either light (laghuvu) or heavy (guruvu). Poets classify it using a set of pre-defined rules. This paper formalizes aksharam token, the atomic unit of syllabic classification, as a non-deterministic finite automaton (NFA) with the regular expression$\colon$ $(A_h+A_d+A_p)(\epsilon+V_s)+A_m+H^+G(\epsilon+H+V_s+V_v)$, where $\epsilon$ denotes a null string, $A$ denotes a vowel (achchu), comprising hrasvam ($A_h$), deergham ($A_d$), plutham ($A_p$), and miscellaneous ($A_m$), $H$ a pure consonant (pollu\_hallu), $G$ a vowel diacritic (gunintha\_chihnam), $V_s$ the sunna (anusvara), and $V_v$ the visarga, the latter two being nasal and aspirated sounds respectively. We then present automata diagrams and regular expressions for (i) a necessary condition satisfied by every light letter, and (ii) a sufficient condition for a letter to be heavy. Finally, we propose graphical visualizations for the 9 Telugu poem types.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes Telugu metrical poetry's atomic syllabic unit (aksharam token) as a non-deterministic finite automaton (NFA) with an explicit regular expression, and provides automata for light and heavy syllable conditions alongside visualizations for nine Telugu poem types.
AI.motivation: Telugu metrical poetry relies on classifying every aksharam token as light (laghuvu) or heavy (guruvu) via pre-defined rules that benefit from formal automata-theoretic specification.
AI.method: The authors formalize the aksharam token as an NFA with a regular expression over vowels, pure consonants, diacritics, sunna, and visarga, derive automata and regular expressions for necessary light-letter and sufficient heavy-letter conditions, and design graphical visualizations for nine poem types.
AI.result: The paper delivers a formal NFA specification, regular expressions for light and heavy syllabic conditions, and graphical visualizations covering all nine Telugu poem types.
AI.conclusion: Formalizing Telugu syllabic weight with NFAs provides a precise computational foundation for analyzing and visualizing Telugu metrical poetry.

title: Criterion-Activated Preference Synthesis: Attribution-Preserving Preference Data from Explicit Standards
summary: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is notoriously sensitive to attribution ambiguity: when chosen and rejected responses differ along multiple entangled dimensions, the model cannot identify which behavior the preference label teaches. We propose Criterion-Activated Preference Synthesis (CAPS), a criterion-first framework that turns explicit quality standards into attribution-verified preference pairs. CAPS synthesizes contexts and responses from a target criterion, then applies dual-signal scoring: a rubric-bound judge measures criterion compliance, while a blind general judge measures holistic quality. Two filters close the attribution loop: the Empirical Activation Test (EAT) keeps criterion-context pairs where satisfying the criterion improves blind quality, and the Attribution Ratio (AR) keeps pairs whose quality gap is dominated by the target criterion. Instantiated with general rubrics, medical rubrics, and Chinese legal statutes, CAPS shows strong data efficiency and domain transfer. With 20k general synthetic pairs, it outperforms 35k human-annotated HelpSteer3 pairs on IFEval, IFBench, AlpacaEval, and Creative Writing v3. In domain settings, CAPS improves HealthBench with 2k medical pairs and improves Qwen3-8B/14B by +4.9 to +6.6 points on legal benchmarks using only public statutes, without human preference labels. We additionally construct the CAPS-Legal preference dataset.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes Criterion-Activated Preference Synthesis (CAPS), a framework that synthesizes attribution-verified preference pairs from explicit quality standards using dual-signal scoring and two attribution filters. With 20k synthetic pairs, CAPS outperforms 35k human-annotated HelpSteer3 pairs across four benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) suffers from attribution ambiguity when chosen and rejected responses differ across multiple entangled dimensions, obscuring which behavior the preference label teaches.
AI.method: CAPS synthesizes contexts and responses from a target criterion, scores them with both a rubric-bound judge and a blind general judge, and applies the Empirical Activation Test (EAT) and Attribution Ratio (AR) filters to ensure the quality gap is driven by the target criterion.
AI.result: Using 20k general synthetic pairs, CAPS outperforms 35k human-annotated HelpSteer3 pairs on IFEval, IFBench, AlpacaEval, and Creative Writing v3. In domain settings, it improves HealthBench with 2k medical pairs and boosts Qwen3-8B/14B by +4.9 to +6.6 points on legal benchmarks using only public statutes, alongside releasing CAPS-Legal.
AI.conclusion: Criterion-first synthesis with attribution filtering yields highly data-efficient, domain-transferable preference data without human preference labels.

title: Wrong with Confidence: Measuring Hallucination, Overconfidence and Identity-Conditioned Behaviour in Large Language Models
comment: 10 pages, 2 figures. Data and code are included as ancillary files
summary: Large language models answer underspecified questions readily, and accuracy-only evaluation rewards guessing over abstaining. Observational studies link query underspecification to hallucination, but they cannot separate the effect of missing information from item difficulty, and they rarely ask what the model tells the user. We report a pre-registered, paired behavioural study of five open-weight models (Gemma 3 27B, Gemma 4 31B, gpt-oss-120b, Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B and Nemotron 3 Super). Each of 142 factual questions was posed in a fully specified form and in a referentially underspecified form with the same answer key, and three probes measured identity-conditioned behaviour. Two raters scored 5,620 responses under a fixed rubric; effects were estimated with mixed-effects models. Without the referent, the models sought clarification on 33.7% of prompts and answered the rest. Among attempted answers, the error rate rose from 39.1% to 52.0% (mixed-effects odds ratio 4.12, 95% CI 2.76-6.14), and specialist-domain questions failed more often than general ones in every model. Unelicited verbal uncertainty did not track this risk: 75.3% of wrong answers carried no hedge, wrong answers to underspecified prompts were hedged no more often than wrong answers to clear prompts (27.3% vs 22.3%), and hedging separated correct from incorrect answers only weakly (AUROC 0.56). Gendered pronouns followed occupational stereotypes whenever a model committed to one; any stated user identity lengthened answers by about 45% relative to an anonymous user; claimed expertise did not reduce safety caveats. The models either ask or answer as if the question were well posed, and the wording of a guess does not reveal that it is one. Evaluations should score clarification as a distinct outcome and check label validity as well as rater agreement.

AI.tldr: This pre-registered paired study of five open-weight LLMs (5,620 scored responses) shows that referential underspecification increases error rates from 39.1% to 52.0% while unelicited hedging fails to signal uncertainty. Stated user identity lengthens answers by ~45%, and gendered pronouns follow occupational stereotypes.
AI.motivation: Observational studies link query underspecification to hallucination but cannot separate missing information from item difficulty or examine what models communicate to users.
AI.method: The authors pose 142 factual questions in both fully specified and referentially underspecified forms—plus three identity-conditioned probes—to five open-weight models (Gemma 3 27B, Gemma 4 31B, gpt-oss-120b, Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B, and Nemotron 3 Super), with two raters scoring 5,620 responses analyzed via mixed-effects models.
AI.result: Without the referent, models seek clarification on 33.7% of prompts and answer the rest, raising error rates from 39.1% to 52.0% (odds ratio 4.12). Moreover, 75.3% of wrong answers contain no hedge, hedging barely separates correct from incorrect answers (AUROC 0.56), any stated identity lengthens answers by ~45%, and claimed expertise does not reduce safety caveats.
AI.conclusion: LLMs guess confidently on underspecified prompts without signaling uncertainty in their wording, so evaluations must score clarification as a distinct outcome.

title: Mapping the Afterlife of Future Work Statements in NLP Research
summary: Future work statements are one of the few places in scientific papers where authors explicitly describe what they think should happen next. We study what happens to such statements after publication. We construct a dataset of 72,070 future work items extracted from 23,113 ACL Anthology papers published between 1979 and 2025, categorize them by type, retrieve candidate follow-up papers through citation-based and content-based search, and use LLM-based judgments to assess whether later papers pursue the proposed directions. Using this resource, we analyze patterns across time, venues, categories, themes, and authors. We find that many items are later addressed, often within a few years, with clear differences across types and themes and a largely community-driven pattern. Our results suggest that future work statements provide useful evidence for studying how research directions develop in NLP. To support further research, we release our dataset at: this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper constructs a dataset of 72,070 future work items from 23,113 ACL Anthology papers (1979–2025) and uses citation/content search with LLM judgments to track whether later papers pursue them. Many proposed directions are addressed within a few years in a largely community-driven pattern.
AI.motivation: Future work statements capture what authors believe should happen next, yet their post-publication trajectory across NLP research has not been systematically mapped.
AI.method: The authors extract 72,070 future work items from 23,113 ACL Anthology papers, categorize them by type, retrieve candidate follow-up papers via citation-based and content-based search, and apply LLM-based judgments to assess whether later work pursues the proposed directions.
AI.result: Analysis across time, venues, categories, themes, and authors shows that many future work items are addressed within a few years, with distinct variations across types and themes and a predominantly community-driven pattern.
AI.conclusion: Future work statements provide valuable empirical evidence for understanding how research directions evolve in NLP, supported by the authors' public dataset release.
